scenarios.desc: Aperture duty-cycle demonstrator (ground segment & operations).
scenarios.kindDesc: Aperture duty cycle: the navigation-versus-communications time-share a contact plan implies for a pool of steerable apertures. Takes a contact plan (a list of `[[contacts]]` aos_s/los_s windows, each asking for navigation or communications — the same aos_s/los_s vocabulary the `passes` predictor emits), an aperture count, and an ARBITRATION POLICY (navigation-priority by default, or communications-priority, or non-preemptive first-come-first-served), and reports the navigation duty, the communications duty, the idle duty, and the per-session outage — the contact time a session requested and no aperture served. An exact interval sweep over the window boundaries, so touching windows never contend and no aperture-second is double-counted; navigation, communications and idle aperture-seconds are accumulated independently and close against apertures*horizon_s. The report states the resolved policy, its full definition, and the duty and outage definitions, because a duty figure quoted without its arbitration policy is not reproducible. MODELLED scheduling arithmetic: no slew / retune / changeover time is charged when an aperture changes service or session, no data volume, buffer state, energy budget or link closure enters the decision, and the contact windows are inputs — their geometry is whatever produced them. Not a ground-segment scheduling product.
scenarios.toml:
# Aperture duty-cycle demonstrator (ground segment & operations).
#
# How a contact plan divides a pool of steerable apertures between navigation
# (ranging / tracking) and communications (data), and what each session loses when
# more sessions are active than there are apertures.
#
# THE ARBITRATION POLICY IS AN INPUT. A duty figure is only meaningful relative to
# a stated rule for who wins the aperture, so the policy is declared here, echoed
# back in the report with its full definition, and named in the one-line summary.
#   navigation-priority       (default) navigation preempts communications
#   communications-priority             communications preempts navigation
#   first-come-first-served             non-preemptive; the holder keeps the aperture
#
# Re-run with `apertures = 1` to see the one-aperture time-share: on this plan
# navigation is served in full either way and the whole contention loss lands on
# the communications sessions.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED scheduling arithmetic over the supplied windows. No slew /
# retune / changeover time is charged when an aperture changes service or session;
# no data volume, buffer state, energy budget or link closure enters the decision;
# and the contact windows are inputs -- their geometry is whatever produced them
# (the `passes` scenario emits the same aos_s / los_s vocabulary). Not a
# ground-segment scheduling product.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/aperture-duty-cycle.toml
kind = "aperture-duty-cycle"

apertures = 2
arbitration = "navigation-priority"

# The reporting horizon defaults to the plan envelope (earliest aos_s -> latest
# los_s), which is what sets the duty denominator (apertures * horizon_s). Override
# it to score the plan over a fixed operational day instead:
#   horizon_start_s = 0.0
#   horizon_end_s = 86400.0

# The contact plan. ILLUSTRATIVE: three navigation sessions and three
# communications sessions over a 9 000 s envelope, each navigation session
# overlapping a communications one.
[[contacts]]
name = "nav-1"
service = "navigation"
aos_s = 0.0
los_s = 600.0

[[contacts]]
name = "comms-1"
service = "communications"
aos_s = 300.0
los_s = 1500.0

[[contacts]]
name = "nav-2"
service = "navigation"
aos_s = 3600.0
los_s = 4500.0

[[contacts]]
name = "comms-2"
service = "communications"
aos_s = 4200.0
los_s = 6000.0

[[contacts]]
name = "nav-3"
service = "navigation"
aos_s = 7200.0
los_s = 7800.0

[[contacts]]
name = "comms-3"
service = "communications"
aos_s = 7200.0
los_s = 9000.0

scenarios.desc: Dual-constellation ARAIM availability: GPS + Galileo evaluated with the advanced ARAIM engine, including the constellation-wide fault hypothesis (`araim_dual`).
scenarios.kindDesc: Snapshot / solution-separation / ARAIM RAIM with HPL/VPL and a Stanford diagram.
scenarios.toml:
# Dual-constellation ARAIM availability: GPS + Galileo evaluated with the advanced
# ARAIM engine, including the constellation-wide fault hypothesis (`araim_dual`).
#
# Unlike `integrity-raim.toml` (single-constellation solution-separation RAIM), this
# runs `araim_dual_raim` at every epoch over a combined GPS + Galileo geometry: the
# fault-free, single-satellite, AND per-constellation fault hypotheses all feed one
# MHSS integrity-risk budget (P_HMI). The primary constellation is fault group 0 and
# each `[[constellations]]` entry the next group.
#
# Constellation-fault-robust integrity (staying safe even if an entire constellation
# fails) is the demanding mode: under the constellation-fault hypothesis the residual
# constellation must carry the fix alone, so it always costs availability relative to
# pooling. How much depends on the sky. On the real 2026-06-07 GPS + Galileo catalogue,
# evaluated at one common epoch, it still reaches 0.990 at a 12 m VAL against 1.000
# pooled (tests/araim_dual_real_data.rs) — two full constellations can carry it; a
# depleted one is where a third constellation or SBAS augmentation earns its place.
# The numerically exact EU ARAIM TN Table A-3 reproduction is an external follow-on
# (docs/ARAIM_REFERENCE.md).
kind = "integrity"

mask_deg = 5.0
sigma_uere_m = 0.75   # ISM σ_URA (dual-frequency, m)
p_fa = 1.0e-5         # false-alarm / continuity budget
p_md = 1.0e-3
al_h_m = 40.0         # horizontal alert limit (APV-I)
al_v_m = 50.0         # vertical alert limit (APV-I)
araim_dual = true     # advanced dual-/multi-constellation ARAIM
p_hmi = 1.0e-7        # per-axis integrity-risk budget

[time]
step_s = 300.0
duration_s = 43200.0  # 12 h

[user]
altitude_km = 0.4
inclination_deg = 45.0
raan_deg = 10.0
u0_deg = 0.0

[constellation]       # GPS-like Walker 24/6/1
altitude_km = 20200.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 1.0

[[constellations]]    # Galileo-like Walker 24/3/1
altitude_km = 23222.0
inclination_deg = 56.0
planes = 3
sats_per_plane = 8
phasing_f = 1.0

scenarios.desc: The engine's ARAIM protection levels against the WG-C subgroup's OWN worked examples.
scenarios.kindDesc: Published ARAIM certification reference vectors: the engine's ARAIM horizontal and vertical protection levels run against the WG-C ARAIM Technical Subgroup's OWN worked numerical examples, at the tolerance (TOL_PL = 5e-2 m) those documents themselves state. Two vectors are committed as fixtures, each carrying its retrieval URL, retrieval date, source-file SHA-256 and page: the Reference Airborne Algorithm Description Document v3.1 (2019) Appendix D — self-consistent, and the acceptance vector — and the Milestone 3 Report (2016) Annex A section A.IX, the statement the research bibliographies cite. Every published input (the 10-satellite 2-constellation geometry matrix, the C_int and C_acc variance diagonals, b_nom, P_sat, P_const and the LPV-200 constant set) and every published output (VPL, HPL, EMT, sigma_v_acc, K_fa_3 and the two constellation-fault modes' sigma_3, sigma_ss_3 and b_3) is reported beside the engine's own number and their absolute difference. The protection-level equation is NOT re-solved here: the reference's mode list is handed to the engine's existing raim::araim_protection_level / araim_integrity_risk, so the bisection and the Gaussian-tail algebra under test are the engine's own; only the geometry, the sub-solutions, the detection thresholds and the published budget split are built for it. EXTERNALLY CHECKED against the 2019 vector: VPL 18.2926 m vs 18.3 m published, HPL 13.4063 m vs 13.45 m, EMT 7.2997 m vs 7.2998 m, sigma_v_acc 1.3694 m vs 1.3694 m, and all six published intermediates to within half a unit in their last printed decimal. The 2016 vector carries two internal defects the report states rather than hides — a sign typo in row 3 of G, and a K_fa_3 evaluated at 57 fault modes while the document states N_fault_max = 1 (12 modes) — so its geometry intermediates reproduce exactly while its protection levels are reported as measured discrepancies and excluded from the acceptance figure; the tolerance is never widened to absorb them. Every emitted numeric field carries a unit and a provenance class, and a transcribed figure is labelled `published` so it can never be mistaken for a computed one. SCOPE: only N_fault_max = 1 (single-satellite and single-constellation fault modes) is implemented, and a case whose priors require simultaneous multi-event fault subsets is REFUSED rather than silently truncated; fault detection, exclusion, the chi-square consistency check and the double-counting re-allocation step of the reference algorithm are out of scope. This reproduces a published reference algorithm's worked example — it is not a certification, an airworthiness artefact or an approval.
scenarios.toml:
# The engine's ARAIM protection levels against the WG-C subgroup's OWN worked examples.
#
# This is an EXTERNAL check, not a self-test: two published certification reference vectors
# are committed as fixtures, each carrying its retrieval URL, retrieval date, source-file
# SHA-256 and page number, and the engine's numbers are run against them at the tolerance
# (TOL_PL = 5e-2 m) those documents themselves state.
#
#   * Reference Airborne Algorithm Description Document v3.1 (2019), Appendix D — internally
#     self-consistent, and the acceptance vector.
#   * Milestone 3 Report (2016), Annex A section A.IX — the statement the research
#     bibliographies cite.
#
# Every published input (the 10-satellite 2-constellation geometry matrix, the C_int and
# C_acc variance diagonals, b_nom, P_sat, P_const and the LPV-200 constant set) and every
# published output (VPL, HPL, EMT, sigma_v_acc, K_fa_3, and each constellation-fault mode's
# sigma_3, sigma_ss_3 and b_3) is reported beside the engine's own number and their absolute
# difference. A transcribed figure is labelled `published` so it can never be mistaken for a
# computed one.
#
# The protection-level equation is NOT re-solved here. The reference's mode list is handed
# to the engine's existing raim::araim_protection_level / araim_integrity_risk, so the
# bisection and the Gaussian-tail algebra under test are the engine's own; only the geometry,
# the sub-solutions, the detection thresholds and the published budget split are built for it.
#
# RESULT against the 2019 vector: VPL 18.2926 m vs 18.3 m published, HPL 13.4063 m vs
# 13.45 m, EMT 7.2997 m vs 7.2998 m, sigma_v_acc 1.3694 m vs 1.3694 m, and all six published
# intermediates to within half a unit in their last printed decimal.
#
# The 2016 vector carries two internal defects the report STATES rather than hides — a sign

#
# SCOPE: only N_fault_max = 1 (single-satellite and single-constellation fault modes) is

#
# Omit `vector` to run both; set it to select one.

kind = "araim-reference-check"

scenarios.desc: 3-DOF attitude & pointing error budget demonstrator (pre-hardware AOCS/GNC).
scenarios.kindDesc: 3-DOF attitude & pointing error budget: the worst-case gravity-gradient disturbance torque ((3/2)(μ/R³)ΔI) and a root-sum-square pointing-error budget over named 1σ contributors (sensor noise, reaction-wheel jitter, thermal, alignment) with the dominant term, for an orbit altitude + body inertia spread. MODELLED scalar AOCS budget — a pre-hardware complement to Basilisk/42, not a control-loop/6-DoF/flexible-mode simulation.
scenarios.toml:
# 3-DOF attitude & pointing error budget demonstrator (pre-hardware AOCS/GNC).
#
# The worst-case gravity-gradient disturbance torque ((3/2)(mu/R^3)*dI) and a
# root-sum-square pointing-error budget over named 1-sigma contributors, with the
# dominant term -- a scalar pointing figure of merit to bracket before committing
# to a control design.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: MODELLED scalar error budget -- a pre-hardware complement to
# Basilisk/42, NOT a control-loop / 6-DoF / flexible-mode simulation. The
# gravity-gradient term is reported as a torque (mapping it to pointing needs a
# control stiffness the caller owns); the budget is the quadrature sum of the
# supplied 1-sigma contributors.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/attitude-budget.toml
kind = "attitude-budget"

altitude_km = 600.0
i_max_kg_m2 = 100.0
i_min_kg_m2 = 60.0

[[contributors]]
name = "star_tracker_noise"
sigma_arcsec = 5.0
[[contributors]]
name = "reaction_wheel_jitter"
sigma_arcsec = 8.0
[[contributors]]
name = "thermal_distortion"
sigma_arcsec = 4.0
[[contributors]]
name = "alignment"
sigma_arcsec = 3.0

scenarios.desc: Road vehicle through an urban canyon: GNSS/INS dead-reckoning across an underpass and a roadside jammer, against a lane-level budget.
scenarios.kindDesc: Loosely- and tightly-coupled GNSS/INS error-state EKF.
scenarios.toml:
# Road vehicle through an urban canyon: GNSS/INS dead-reckoning across an underpass and
# a roadside jammer, against a lane-level budget.
#
# The mission question a driver-assistance or automated-driving team asks: a car's
# Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver loses the sky under an overpass and
# then again near a roadside jammer (a low-power in-vehicle "privacy" jammer on a
# neighbouring vehicle is the common case). How long does the fused GNSS/inertial
# navigation system (INS) solution stay inside half a lane? The 1.5 m threshold is half
# a 3.5 m lane less a margin, a budget chosen here, not a standard's figure.
#
# The pack is `gnss-ins`: a three-axis strapdown navigator disciplined by a 15-state
# error-state extended Kalman filter (EKF), then coasting through the outages. The
# GNSS timeline: open sky for 60 s, a 15 s underpass, 45 s of open sky, then 60 s
# near the jammer.
#
# The pack has two fixed slots named `imu_quantum` and `imu_classical`. Here
# `imu_quantum` carries the BETTER unit, a tactical-grade comparator, and
# `imu_classical` carries an automotive MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical system) unit.
# Nothing quantum is modelled in this file. Both use the representative class
# coefficients from the engine's grade table (Groves 2013, Table 4.1 band; the same
# figures as `imu_grade` in `ins-trn-coast`), NOT a datasheet for any part:
#   - tactical: accelerometer bias 300 ug = 2.94e-3 m/s^2, gyro bias 1 deg/h =
#     4.848e-6 rad/s;
#   - industrial (automotive MEMS sits in this band): accelerometer bias 3000 ug =
#     2.94e-2 m/s^2, gyro bias 20 deg/h = 9.696e-5 rad/s, accelerometer scale factor
#     2000 ppm.
#
# Honest scope (inherited from the `gnss-ins` pack): loosely coupled, the pack's single
# deterministic driving profile (a forward-acceleration and yaw square wave), not a
# recorded drive; no odometer or wheel-speed aiding (the engine has none), no
# multipath model, and constant biases, which the filter can learn while GNSS is up,
# so the coast is a best case for these classes. MODELLED: every figure is modelled.
kind = "gnss-ins"
seed = 7
threshold_m = 1.5
fix_interval_s = 1.0
sigma_pos_m = 1.0
sigma_vel_mps = 0.05
lat_deg = 48.137
lon_deg = 11.575
alt_m = 520.0

[time]
step_s = 0.1
duration_s = 180.0

[gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0,   t1 = 60.0,  state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 60.0,  t1 = 75.0,  state = "denied" },
  { t0 = 75.0,  t1 = 120.0, state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 120.0, t1 = 180.0, state = "denied" },
]

[imu_quantum]
id = "tactical-imu"
provenance = "Tactical-grade class (Groves 2013 Table 4.1 band, engine grade table): accel bias 300 ug = 2.94e-3 m/s^2, gyro bias 1 deg/h = 4.848e-6 rad/s; signs chosen"
accel_bias = [2.94e-3, -2.94e-3, 0.0]
gyro_bias = [0.0, 0.0, 4.848e-6]

[imu_quantum.filter_prior]
sigma_accel_bias = 2.94e-3
sigma_gyro_bias = 4.848e-6

[imu_classical]
id = "automotive-mems"
provenance = "Industrial-grade class, where automotive MEMS units sit (Groves 2013 Table 4.1 band, engine grade table): accel bias 3000 ug = 2.94e-2 m/s^2, gyro bias 20 deg/h = 9.696e-5 rad/s; signs chosen"
accel_bias = [2.94e-2, -2.94e-2, 0.0]
gyro_bias = [9.696e-5, -9.696e-5, 9.696e-5]

[imu_classical.filter_prior]
sigma_accel_bias = 2.94e-2
sigma_gyro_bias = 9.696e-5

# The class's accelerometer scale-factor error (2000 ppm) layered on the constant bias.
[imu_classical.error_model]
scale_accel_ppm = [2000.0, 2000.0, 2000.0]

scenarios.desc: A chained mission: nominal, jamming, spoofing, GNSS loss with clock holdover and inertial coasting, an integrity alarm, and recovery, on one shared timeline.
scenarios.kindDesc: Campaign: existing scenario kinds composed into one run, with every number read from a real run of the named kind. Four sections, in any combination. PHASES: a chained mission on one shared timeline -- each phase runs one or more scenarios (for example jamming, then spoofing, then a clock in holdover with an inertial navigation system coasting beside it, then an integrity alarm, then recovery), their outputs are read into named channels (clock time error against its guard, carrier-to-noise density ratio against the tracking floor, protection level against the alert limit, position error, satellites tracking, alarm flags) by a per-kind preset or by explicit result paths, and resampled onto a common grid by zero-order hold, with phase boundaries and events; state is handed on by carry (a channel continues from the previous phase's end value), handoff (a previous phase's number written into this phase's scenario) and end_at (a phase ends at a time a run computed, such as a spoofing monitor's detection time). SWEEP: a grid over one to three dotted scenario keys of any kind (a whole-number segment indexes an array of tables, as in system.2.sisre_m), with metrics read by result path and, with runs above one, a seeded Monte Carlo ensemble at every node. MONTE_CARLO: realisation k runs at base_seed + k; each metric reports mean, standard deviation, nearest-rank 5th/50th/95th percentiles and a fixed-seed bootstrap 95% confidence interval on the mean. COMPOSE: several scenarios under shared values (one jammer's power and position written into a maritime and a road receiver), with a combined best/worst summary. The result carries a campaign hash, a digest over every member result, and a units entry for every emitted number; the interoperability exports write each member scenario that has geometry as its own file set. Composition identities are tested: a one-phase campaign reproduces the stand-alone run bit for bit, a fixed-seed ensemble is byte-stable, and on a white-frequency-noise clock the ensemble mean falls inside the reported interval with the spread matching sqrt(q_wf * tau). MODELLED: the additive carry and the zero-order hold are modelling choices, and each phase carries the label of the kind that ran it.
scenarios.toml:
# A chained mission: nominal, jamming, spoofing, GNSS loss with clock holdover and
# inertial coasting, an integrity alarm, and recovery, on one shared timeline.
#
# Every phase runs ordinary scenarios of existing kinds, each dispatched exactly as
# `kshana <file>.toml` would run it. The campaign reads their outputs into channels
# on one mission timeline (a 10 s grid, zero-order hold) and draws them as synced
# panels: clock time error against its guard, the carrier-to-noise density ratio
# (C/N0) against the tracking floor, the vertical protection level against the
# alert limit, the inertial position error, and the alarm flags.
#
# State is handed on between phases in two ways here:
# - `end_at`: the spoofing phase ends when the clock-aided spoofing monitor of the
#   `spoof` run detects the ramp (its `classical.detect_time_s`), not at a fixed time.
# - `carry`: the holdover and integrity-alarm phases continue the clock time error
#   from where the previous phase left it, so the offset the spoofer pulled in before
#   detection is where the free-running clock starts. Recovery re-synchronises to
#   GNSS, so it carries nothing.
#
# The receiver is the jamming example's (52 N, 4 E) under a GPS-like 24-satellite
# Walker shell; the jammer is 1 km away and its power sets the phase: off, -30 dBW
# (links degraded but still tracking), 10 dBW (every satellite lost). The clock is a
# chip-scale atomic clock (Microchip SA.45s datasheet sigma_y(1 s) = 3e-10), the
# inertial unit the gnss-ins example's tactical class, and the integrity monitor the
# integrity example's snapshot receiver autonomous integrity monitoring (RAIM) with
# the approach-with-vertical-guidance (APV-I) alert limits, run on that example's
# own user track (a 0.4 km-altitude circular track, not the jamming receiver's
# fixed site). The integrity alarm is produced by a 25 deg elevation mask, standing
# in for the partial sky a receiver has while reacquiring; recovery returns to 5 deg.
#
# MODELLED: the chaining is a modelling choice (additive carry, zero-order hold), and
# each phase is as good as the kind that ran it.
kind = "campaign"
title = "Jamming, spoofing, holdover and integrity: a chained mission"
seed = 20260928

[timeline]
step_s = 10.0

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- nominal
[[phases]]
name = "nominal"
duration_s = 600.0

[[phases.runs]]
[phases.runs.scenario]
seed = 42
threshold_ns = 50.0
[phases.runs.scenario.time]
step_s = 10.0
duration_s = 600.0
[phases.runs.scenario.gnss]
windows = [{ t0 = 0.0, t1 = 600.0, state = "nominal" }]
[phases.runs.scenario.clock_quantum]
id = "optical-sr-lattice"
provenance = "Strontium optical lattice clock, space-oriented goal sigma_y(1s)=1e-15 (arXiv:1503.08457); not flown."
y0 = 5.0e-17
q_wf = 1.0e-30
q_rw = 0.0
[phases.runs.scenario.clock_classical]
id = "csac-sa45s"
provenance = "Microchip SA65 / SA.45s CSAC datasheet sigma_y(1s)=3e-10; q_wf=sigma_y(1s)^2."
y0 = 5.0e-10
q_wf = 9.0e-20
q_rw = 0.0

[[phases.runs]]
[phases.runs.scenario]
kind = "jamming"
seed = 1
mask_deg = 5.0

[phases.runs.scenario.time]
step_s = 30.0

[phases.runs.scenario.receiver]

scenarios.desc: A seeded Monte Carlo ensemble through a campaign, on a case with a closed form.
scenarios.kindDesc: Campaign: existing scenario kinds composed into one run, with every number read from a real run of the named kind. Four sections, in any combination. PHASES: a chained mission on one shared timeline -- each phase runs one or more scenarios (for example jamming, then spoofing, then a clock in holdover with an inertial navigation system coasting beside it, then an integrity alarm, then recovery), their outputs are read into named channels (clock time error against its guard, carrier-to-noise density ratio against the tracking floor, protection level against the alert limit, position error, satellites tracking, alarm flags) by a per-kind preset or by explicit result paths, and resampled onto a common grid by zero-order hold, with phase boundaries and events; state is handed on by carry (a channel continues from the previous phase's end value), handoff (a previous phase's number written into this phase's scenario) and end_at (a phase ends at a time a run computed, such as a spoofing monitor's detection time). SWEEP: a grid over one to three dotted scenario keys of any kind (a whole-number segment indexes an array of tables, as in system.2.sisre_m), with metrics read by result path and, with runs above one, a seeded Monte Carlo ensemble at every node. MONTE_CARLO: realisation k runs at base_seed + k; each metric reports mean, standard deviation, nearest-rank 5th/50th/95th percentiles and a fixed-seed bootstrap 95% confidence interval on the mean. COMPOSE: several scenarios under shared values (one jammer's power and position written into a maritime and a road receiver), with a combined best/worst summary. The result carries a campaign hash, a digest over every member result, and a units entry for every emitted number; the interoperability exports write each member scenario that has geometry as its own file set. Composition identities are tested: a one-phase campaign reproduces the stand-alone run bit for bit, a fixed-seed ensemble is byte-stable, and on a white-frequency-noise clock the ensemble mean falls inside the reported interval with the spread matching sqrt(q_wf * tau). MODELLED: the additive carry and the zero-order hold are modelling choices, and each phase carries the label of the kind that ran it.
scenarios.toml:
# A seeded Monte Carlo ensemble through a campaign, on a case with a closed form.
#
# A chip-scale atomic clock (Microchip SA.45s datasheet sigma_y(1 s) = 3e-10, so a
# white-frequency-noise intensity q_wf = 9e-20 s^2/s and nothing else stochastic) is
# disciplined to GNSS for 600 s and then coasts to 3600 s. The holdover predictor
# removes the deterministic frequency offset exactly, so the time error at the end
# of the run is the accumulated white-frequency noise since the last synchronisation
# at 590 s: Gaussian, mean zero, variance q_wf * tau with tau = 3010 s, a standard
# deviation of sqrt(9e-20 * 3010) s = 16.46 ns (NIST Technical Note 1337, the random
# walk of phase under white frequency noise).
#
# Realisation k runs the scenario with `seed = 42 + k`, so the ensemble reproduces
# exactly. The campaign reports, per metric, the mean, the standard deviation, the
# 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles and a fixed-seed bootstrap 95% confidence interval
# on the mean. The test suite checks that the mean falls inside that interval around
# zero and that the spread matches 16.46 ns.
#
# MODELLED: the clock is a datasheet-level model, not a measurement of any unit.
kind = "campaign"
title = "Monte Carlo: free-running clock error against its closed form"
seed = 20260928

[monte_carlo]
runs = 200
seed_key = "seed"
metrics = [
  { name = "final_error", path = "classical.series[-1].error_ns" },
  { name = "timing_rms", path = "classical.fom.timing_rms_ns" },
]

[monte_carlo.scenario]
seed = 42
threshold_ns = 20.0
[monte_carlo.scenario.time]
step_s = 10.0
duration_s = 3600.0
[monte_carlo.scenario.gnss]
windows = [
  { t0 = 0.0, t1 = 600.0, state = "nominal" },
  { t0 = 600.0, t1 = 3600.0, state = "denied" },
]
[monte_carlo.scenario.clock_quantum]
id = "optical-sr-lattice"
provenance = "Strontium optical lattice clock, space-oriented goal sigma_y(1s)=1e-15 (arXiv:1503.08457); not flown."
y0 = 5.0e-17
q_wf = 1.0e-30
q_rw = 0.0
[monte_carlo.scenario.clock_classical]
id = "csac-sa45s"
provenance = "Microchip SA65 / SA.45s CSAC datasheet sigma_y(1s)=3e-10; q_wf=sigma_y(1s)^2."
y0 = 5.0e-10
q_wf = 9.0e-20
q_rw = 0.0

MONTE_CARLO: realisation k runs at base_seed + k; each metric reports mean, standard deviation, nearest-rank 5th/50th/95th percentiles and a fixed-seed bootstrap 95% confidence interval on the mean. COMPOSE: several scenarios under shared values (one jammer's power and position written into a maritime and a road receiver), with a combined best/worst summary. The result carries a campaign hash, a digest over every member result, and a units entry for every emitted number; the interoperability exports write each member scenario that has geometry as its own file set. Composition identities are tested: a one-phase campaign reproduces the stand-alone run bit for bit, a fixed-seed ensemble is byte-stable, and on a white-frequency-noise clock the ensemble mean falls inside the reported interval with the spread matching sqrt(q_wf * tau). scenarios.toml:
# A chained mission driven by the L-band spectrum: a chirp jammer takes GPS L1 C/A and
# Galileo E1, the clock holds over, and a continuous-wave (CW) tone left on the L1
# carrier keeps C/A down while E1 recovers, so the receiver falls back to Galileo and
# its integrity monitor runs on a Galileo-only sky.
#
# Every phase runs ordinary scenarios of existing kinds, each dispatched exactly as
# `kshana <file>.toml` would run it. The carrier-to-noise density ratio (C/N0) of each
# band comes from the `spectrum` kind: the jammer's spectral separation coefficient
# against that band's own modulation, through (C/N0)_eff = [1/(C/N0) + sum (J/S) kappa]^-1
# (see docs/SPECTRUM.md). The campaign reads the L1 C/A and E1 rows of the spectrum
# timeline into two channels on one mission timeline (a 1 s grid, zero-order hold).
#
# State is handed on between phases in two ways here:
# - `end_at`: the onset phase ends when the spectrum run first loses L1 C/A
#   (`timeline.bands[0].first_loss_t_s`, 10 s here), not at a fixed time; the clock's
#   holdover starts at that instant.
# - `carry`: the holdover phase continues the clock time error from the end of the
#   onset phase. The fallback phase re-synchronises the clock to Galileo, so it
#   carries nothing.
#
# The jammers are the ones in scenarios/l-band-waterfall-jamming.toml: a 16 MHz chirp
# privacy device at -13 dBW EIRP, 100 m away, and a CW tone on 1575.42 MHz at -20 dBW
# EIRP, 1 km away, both through the jamming kind's free-space path loss. The clock is
# a chip-scale atomic clock (Microchip SA.45s datasheet sigma_y(1 s) = 3e-10). The
# integrity monitor is the integrity example's snapshot receiver autonomous integrity
# monitoring (RAIM) with the approach-with-vertical-guidance (APV-I) alert limits, on
# a GPS-like 24-satellite Walker shell during onset and on a Galileo-like Walker
# 24/3/1 (29 599.8 km semi-major axis, 56 deg; Galileo OS SDD 1.1) during fallback.
#
# MODELLED: the chaining is a modelling choice (additive carry, zero-order hold), and
# each phase is as good as the kind that ran it. E1 recovering under the CW tone rests
# on the spectrum kind's continuous-spectrum treatment (a CW tone on the MBOC carrier
# null couples nothing); a real tone would couple through the code's spectral lines.
kind = "campaign"
title = "L-band jamming from the spectrum, clock holdover and a Galileo-only fallback"
seed = 20260928

[timeline]
step_s = 1.0

# loss of L1 C/A that the spectrum run computes.

duration_s = 60.0
end_at = "timeline.bands[0].first_loss_t_s"
end_at_run = 1

[[phases.runs]]

[phases.runs.scenario.time]

scenarios.toml:
# A parameter sweep through a campaign: the jamming example's receiver (52 N, 4 E,
# GPS-like 24-satellite Walker shell) under a broadband jammer 1 km away, with the
# jammer's transmit power swept from -50 dBW (10 nW) to +10 dBW (10 W) in 5 dB
# steps. Each node is an ordinary `jamming` run; the campaign records, per node,
# the fraction of epochs with at least four satellites still tracking, the mean
# jammer-to-signal ratio (J/S), and the fewest satellites tracking.
#
# The jamming chain (Kaplan and Hegarty, Understanding GPS/GNSS, 3rd ed., section
# 9.4) is deterministic, so one run per node is the whole answer; add `runs` and a
# `seed_key` to make every node a Monte Carlo ensemble for a stochastic kind.
# J/S moves exactly 1 dB per dB of transmit power; availability falls from 1 to 0
# where the effective carrier-to-noise density ratio crosses the 25 dB-Hz floor.
#
# MODELLED: as the `jamming` kind is.

title = "Jammer power sweep: availability and J/S against transmit power"
seed = 20260928

[sweep]

  { name = "availability", path = "fom.availability_under_jamming" },
  { name = "mean_js", path = "fom.mean_js_db" },

scenarios.desc: Celeste IOD signal designs: the frequency bands and the "Classical Pilot" signal configuration #1 of ESA's Celeste In-Orbit Demonstration (IOD) low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) mission, as parameterised signal designs.
scenarios.kindDesc: LEO-PNT signal designs: parameterised low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) signals for any system, band and structure. A SIGNAL is a band (centre frequency, transmit bandwidth, ITU allocation RNSS/RDSS/MSS/EESS/non-RNSS/other) and components (acquisition, data, pilot; any subset), each with a modulation (BPSK(n) with fractional n, BOC(m,n), MBOC(6,1,p) or a flat OFDM-like band), a power share, optional FDMA sub-carrier offsets, a code length and a data rate. Signals come from compiled-in public preset files (xona-pulsar, iridium-stl, starlink-soo, centispace, generic-c-band, generic-bands; each with its source URL and every unpublished value labelled REPRESENTATIVE) or are written inline. PER SIGNAL: the band-limited power spectral density and the fraction of each component's power the transmit band passes (BPSK closed form beside the numeric value), the RMS (Gabor) bandwidth, the delay-lock-loop code-tracking thermal-noise jitter against C/N0 and early-late spacing from the band-limited coherent (or non-coherent) early-late formula of Betz & Kolodziejski 2009 with its unlimited-band textbook form and its vanishing-spacing Gabor bound, the ranging accuracy in metres, the acquisition search space (Doppler bins from the orbit's maximum Doppler plus oscillator and user terms, times code bins), square-law detection probability and the mean serial and code-parallel acquisition time, the spectral separation coefficient of the signal into GPS L1 C/A, Galileo E1, GPS L5, Galileo E5a, E5b and E5 AltBOC and of each into the signal with the C/N0 degradation, and the CW, wideband and matched J/S the tracked component tolerates, from the spectrum kind's own SSC machinery. A BAND TRADE: first-order ionospheric delay (40.3 TEC/f^2), free-space loss, ranging accuracy at equal C/N0 and at equal EIRP, and jammer tolerance. Optional SHAPE CHECKS hold a design's spectrum against a described measurement (MODELLED consistency). VALIDATED: the BPSK power-in-band (90.3 % in the main lobe) and Gabor-bandwidth closed forms, the band-limited jitter reducing to the textbook coherent early-late form and to its Gabor bound, the offset BPSK spectral separation coefficient against its Parseval closed form, the AltBOC spectrum's unit area, and the maximum LEO Doppler against the published Xona Pulsar (32-34 kHz) and Iridium (36 kHz) figures. MODELLED: every design, power split, C/N0 and jammer level; EFQPSK, CSK and OFDM spectra are approximated.
scenarios.toml:
# Celeste IOD signal designs: the frequency bands and the "Classical Pilot" signal
# configuration #1 of ESA's Celeste In-Orbit Demonstration (IOD) low Earth orbit (LEO)
# positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) mission, as parameterised signal designs.
#
# THIS FILE IS THE ONLY PLACE IN THE REPOSITORY THAT HOLDS WORKSHOP-DERIVED NUMBERS.
# Every carrier, bandwidth, allocation, component structure and shape target below
# marked WORKSHOP was presented at the ESA NAVISP LEO-PNT workshop, 2026 (the
# Navigation Innovation and Support Programme), and cleared for use; no Celeste signal
# specification is public. Nothing else in the engine depends on this file, and nothing
# compiles it in (it is a repository-only scenario, not bundled into the binary):
# deleting it removes Celeste from a release, and every other scenario, test and oracle
# still runs. See docs/LEO-SIGNAL.md.
#
# What the IOD is for, in ESA's own public words: an in-orbit demonstration of 11
# satellites plus a spare that tests radionavigation signals in several bands
# (https://www.esa.int/Applications/Satellite_navigation/Celeste/Celeste_IOD_-_Facts_and_figures).
# The IOD signals are a vehicle for experiments; later phases (Celeste In-Orbit
# Pathfinder, a European Union LEO-PNT layer) will use their own signal designs, which
# is why these are presets of a general signal model, not "the Celeste signal".
#
# Bands presented (WORKSHOP), with the ITU service allocation:
#   E5    1191.795 MHz  RNSS      51.15 MHz  (the Galileo E5 centre; 5 x 10.23 MHz wide)
#   SR    2492.028 MHz  RDSS      15 MHz
#   SM    2170.00 MHz   MSS       0.2 MHz and 5 MHz (for 5G non-terrestrial-network terminals)
#   UHF   465.465 MHz   EESS      10 MHz
#   C     5019.861 MHz  RNSS      19.7 MHz
#   Cext  5071.011 MHz (B1) and 5122.161 MHz (B2), non-RNSS, 120 MHz and 240 MHz
# (RNSS Radio Navigation Satellite Service, RDSS Radio Determination Satellite Service,
# MSS Mobile Satellite Service, EESS Earth Exploration-Satellite Service.)
#
# Configuration #1, "Classical Pilot" (WORKSHOP), BPSK(n) = binary phase-shift keying at
# n x 1.023 Mchip/s, FDMA = frequency-division multiple access:
#   E5#1   pilot BPSK(10); data PfA BPSK(1) or PfB BPSK(10); no acquisition component
#   S#1    pilot BPSK(5);  data BPSK(1) FDMA; acquisition BPSK(1/3) FDMA
#   UHF#1  as S#1
#   CR#1   pilot BPSK(10); data BPSK(10); acquisition BPSK(1/3)
#
# ASSUMPTIONS (not presented, each labelled on its component): the power splits (pilot
# 50 %, the rest shared equally); the code lengths (one 1 ms period; BPSK(1/3) over 1 ms
# is 341 chips); the FDMA sub-carrier offsets (S#1 at -6.0 and -3.3 MHz, where the
# measured IOD S-band spectrum shown at the workshop has narrow components, which
# component sits on which being an assumption; UHF#1 at -4.0 and -2.2 MHz, scaled to the
# 10 MHz band); and, for the SM and Cext bands, whose modulation was not presented, a
# REPRESENTATIVE single BPSK component sized to the band. The orbit altitude, 510 km,
# is public (GMV, https://www.ion.org/gnss/abstracts.cfm?paperID=16907; Thales Alenia
# Space press release).
#
# The [[shape_checks]] entry holds the E5#1 PfA design's band-limited spectrum against
# the measured IOD E5 spectrum shown at the workshop: a narrow central BPSK(1)-like peak
# on a BPSK(10)-like main lobe with nulls near +/-10 MHz, and sidelobes near +/-15 MHz
# some 22 to 25 dB below the peak (IOD-1 peaked near -133 dBW/Hz, sidelobes about -155 to
# -158 dBW/Hz). MODELLED consistency only: the measurement has no published calibration,
# so shapes are compared, not levels.
#
# The C/N0 sweep reaches 57.5 dB-Hz, the peak of the IOD pass shown at the workshop
# (a bell-shaped pass from about 41 to 57.5 dB-Hz over some 200 s, 7 to 10 dB above the
# Galileo satellites tracked beside it).
kind = "leo-signal"

[receiver]
noise_figure_db = 2.0
antenna_temp_k = 290.0
cn0_dbhz = [40.0, 45.0, 50.0, 55.0, 57.5]
reference_cn0_dbhz = 50.0
loop_bandwidth_hz = 1.0
integration_time_s = 0.02
correlator_spacings_chips = [1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1]
reference_spacing_chips = 0.5
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0

[acquisition]
altitude_km = 510.0
oscillator_ppm = 0.5
coherent_ms = 1.0
noncoherent = 1
pfa_cell = 1e-4

[trade]
reference_signal = "celeste-iod-e5-1-pfa"
slant_tec_tecu = 50.0
slant_range_km = 1000.0

[[signals]]
name = "celeste-iod-e5-1-pfa"
system = "Celeste IOD"
source = "WORKSHOP"
source_ref = "presented at the ESA NAVISP LEO-PNT workshop, 2026"
centre_mhz = 1191.795
tx_bandwidth_mhz = 51.15

scenarios.desc: GNSS positioning joined by the two ESA Celeste in-orbit demonstration satellites.
scenarios.kindDesc: Fused medium-Earth-orbit (MEO) and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) over ANY constellations: each [[system]] is a GNSS preset of the constellation-design kind, a LEO preset (xona-pulsar, iridium-stl, starlink-sop, centispace, generic-c-band, the atomic-zero-clock ephemeris model, or another preset file, each in its own file with its sources marked PUBLIC, WORKSHOP or DERIVED), Walker shells or explicit element sets, with a carrier, a chip rate, a carrier-to-noise density (C/N0) envelope from the elevation mask to the zenith, a signal-in-space range error (SISRE), a Doppler sigma and a clock model (its own receiver clock, so the inter-system bias is estimated, or a known broadcast offset). Four modes. DOPPLER: batch Gauss-Newton positioning from range rate with analytic partials, clock-drift and optional velocity states and an optional height constraint, single- or multi-satellite, the error against window length, the Doppler, Doppler-rate and jerk envelope of each LEO system, and the single-pass along-track and cross-track accuracy against the cross-track offset (the cross-track error grows without bound as the pass goes overhead; a single pass also has a mirror solution across the ground track). A Doppler-only signal of opportunity (starlink-sop) runs here. JOINT: per-epoch weighted least-squares pseudorange fixes from GNSS alone, LEO alone and both, per-measurement sigmas from a delay-lock-loop thermal-noise model at C/N0 plus the SISRE (or a fixed sigma, so a signal model can feed them), the estimated inter-system biases, and PDOP/HDOP/VDOP against the number of LEO satellites added. POLAR: satellites in view and DOP against latitude for GNSS, LEO and both. TIMING: time transfer to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) from LEO satellites at a known position with a two-state clock filter whose process noise comes from the engine's oscillator classes, against C/N0 and the oscillator, and the IS-GPS-200 system-time-to-UTC expression; with [timing] trace = true every row also reports its time error and predicted sigma at every epoch. VALIDATED: the largest Doppler of an overhead-to-horizon pass against the published Iridium (up to 36 kHz) and Xona Pulsar X1 (32 to 34 kHz) figures. MODELLED: everything else; the DOP is checked against a hand-derived case, the fixes against their covariance, and the Doppler model against the range-acceleration identity.

# abstract 16907). This file and src/leo_fusion/presets/celeste_iod.rs can be deleted

scenarios.desc: Independent-estimator test of the cislunar arc-length observability threshold (R6, paper B).
scenarios.kindDesc: MODELLED independent-estimator test of the cislunar arc-length observability threshold. That threshold is a RANK read on the observability matrix assembled from the ANALYTIC range Jacobian rows and the ANALYTIC variational state-transition matrix, and its square-root-information-filter cross-check folds those same rows — a consistency check between two numerical machines, not corroboration. This kind supplies the missing arbiter: a batch least-squares estimator that actually RECOVERS the chief's initial state from simulated measurements, with the measurement partials taken as CENTRAL FINITE DIFFERENCES of the composed forward model. It calls no analytic Jacobian row, no variational STM, no singular-value or eigen decomposition, no rank tolerance and no square-root information filter — a source-text guard in tests/cislunar_arc_recovery_reference.rs makes that enforceable — while the dynamics (the same RK4 CR3BP flow), the initial conditions (the same differential-corrected constellation), the scalar observable and the epoch grid are shared deliberately and named in the emitted `independence` block, because two analyses of one physical problem must agree about the physics to be comparable. Two criteria, each swept over five decades of its own bound: NOISE-FREE RECOVERY (every seeded trial's final state error at most recovery_factor times its a-priori displacement — the rank analogue, with no singular-value tolerance in it) and MONTE-CARLO ESTIMABILITY (the measured RMS position error over a seeded noise ensemble below a stated bound — the estimability analogue, measured rather than predicted). Supports the planar four-state and the spatial six-state, the DRO / L2 halo / L2 NRHO families, range and range-rate observables, and a Moon-centred polar parameterisation in which the transformation is applied to the STATE and the forward model re-differenced there. MEASURED on the published planar DRO grid: the estimator recovers the four-state from 0.782609 h against the rank criterion's 2.086957 h at rel_tol 1e-6 (ratio 0.375) — the rank threshold is NOT corroborated as a recoverability boundary — while the measured estimability boundary lands in the same grid cell as the formal one, 5.739130 h, and the measured error curve reproduces the formal 1-sigma over 21 arc lengths to a geometric-mean ratio of 0.98. MODELLED: the constellation design, the epoch grid, the single tracked link, the displacement magnitude, the measurement sigma and the two stated bounds. Not a certified navigation-performance product.

scenarios.desc: Planar cislunar constellation observability over a tracking arc (P6).
scenarios.kindDesc: MODELLED planar cislunar constellation observability (P6): tracks a four-spacecraft differential-corrected planar-DRO constellation with inter-satellite ranging and reports how much of a spacecraft's four-state [x,y,ẋ,ẏ] the arc makes observable. Emits (1) the rank-vs-arc-length table for a single range-only link — instantaneously rank-1, growing toward the full four-state as the arc extends (P6 Table 1); (2) the observability-Gramian eigen-spectrum + condition number over the arc; (3) the range-only-vs-range+range-rate instantaneous-rank comparison (the Doppler design lever) plus the range-only-singular / range+rate-defined GDOP reporting; and (4) an independent SRIF cross-validation whose posterior covariance turns finite / well-conditioned exactly at the arc where the observable rank reaches four. VALIDATED core: the observable rank is a rank-revealing singular-value threshold cross-checked against the Gramian eigen-rank; the eigen-spectrum obeys the spectral invariants (trace=Σλ, det=Πλ, Frobenius²=Σλ²); the variational STM is the finite-difference-validated CR3BP STM; the range/range-rate Jacobian rows are finite-difference-validated analytic partials (cross-checked against the crate's 3-D range-rate observable); the four initial conditions are differential-corrected planar DROs that close to a tight periodicity residual and are retrograde; the rank transition is cross-validated against the crate's square-root information filter (posterior covariance finite exactly at full rank, cond(P)=cond(OᵀO)); a rank-deficient snapshot is flagged GDOP-undefined (fim condition=inf), never a bogus finite value — the same singular-geometry guard pvt::solve_spp applies. MODELLED: the constellation design (DRO perilune amplitudes and phases) and the specific rank progression it produces. Not a certified navigation-performance product.
scenarios.toml:
# Planar cislunar constellation observability over a tracking arc (P6).
#
# A small four-spacecraft near-DRO planar constellation near the Moon is tracked by
# inter-satellite ranging. The scenario answers the batch-estimator question: how much of a
# spacecraft's four-state [x, y, xdot, ydot] does the arc actually make observable, and how
# does that grow with arc length? It assembles the observability structure from the crate's
# finite-difference-validated CR3BP variational STM (src/cr3bp.rs) and the analytic
# inter-satellite range / range-rate Jacobians (src/intersat_range.rs), and emits:
#   1. the rank-vs-arc-length table for a single range-only link -- instantaneously rank-1,
#      growing toward the full four-state as the arc lengthens (P6 Table 1);
#   2. the observability-Gramian eigen-spectrum + condition number over the arc; and
#   3. the range-only vs range+range-rate instantaneous-rank comparison (the Doppler design
#      lever) plus range-only-singular / range+rate-defined GDOP reporting.
# (src/cislunar_observability.rs, src/observability_gramian.rs)
#
# Honesty: MODELLED. VALIDATED core -- the observable RANK is a rank-revealing
# singular-value threshold cross-checked against the Gramian eigen-rank; the eigen-spectrum
# obeys the spectral invariants (trace = sum eig, det = prod eig, Frobenius^2 = sum eig^2);
# the variational STM is the finite-difference-validated CR3BP STM; the range / range-rate
# Jacobian rows are finite-difference-validated analytic partials (cross-checked against the
# crate's 3-D range-rate observable); a rank-deficient snapshot is flagged GDOP-undefined
# (fim condition = inf), never a bogus finite value -- the same singular-geometry guard
# pvt::solve_spp applies. MODELLED -- the four near-DRO planar initial conditions (a
# differential-corrected DRO seeder is a follow-on) and the specific rank progression they
# produce. Not a certified navigation-performance product.
kind = "cislunar-observability"

scenarios.desc: Combined gravity + magnetic + terrain GPS-denied navigator — fused alt-PNT.
scenarios.kindDesc: GPS-denied combined gravity + magnetic + terrain navigator: three scalar field channels fused per waypoint for a sharper (lower-CRLB) drift fix than any single field.
scenarios.toml:
# Combined gravity + magnetic + terrain GPS-denied navigator — fused alt-PNT.
#
# The capstone alternative-PNT demo: a vehicle flying with no GNSS takes THREE scalar
# measurements at each waypoint — gravity anomaly (mGal), magnetic-anomaly total intensity
# (nT), and ground elevation (m). For a candidate constant drift offset the joint likelihood
# is the PRODUCT of the three field likelihoods, so the information adds: the joint posterior
# is sharper (a lower CRLB) than any single field. The demo shows a bounded error under 500 m
# over the outage that is never worse than the best single channel — exactly why sensor fusion
# is the path where any one weak field alone would struggle.
#
# Consumed by `kshana::altpnt::terrain::run_combined_altpnt` (and its unit tests), dispatched
# as `kind = "combined-altpnt"`. The gravity field is a low-degree spherical-harmonic trend +
# synthetic mascons; the magnetic channel is the smooth IGRF-14 main field minus its regional
# mean PLUS synthetic crustal-anomaly mascons (the IGRF main field alone is too smooth to
# localise — the real crustal map is a follow-on, see docs/CAPABILITY.md); the terrain channel
# is the self-contained synthetic DEM. Recovery is checked against the INDEPENDENTLY injected
# drift, never any field's own value (non-circular).
#
# NOTE: every top-level scalar key precedes the `[[...]]` array-of-tables blocks — a scalar
# after an array-of-table would be absorbed into that table by TOML.
kind = "combined-altpnt"

# Track + drift + search (shared across the three channels).
start_lat_deg = 12.05
start_lon_deg = 20.05
step_lat_deg = 0.004
step_lon_deg = 0.003
waypoints = 60

drift_lat_deg = 0.5
drift_lon_deg = -0.4

search_half_deg = 0.8
search_step_deg = 0.08
refine_stages = 3
refine_factor = 8.0
noise_seed = 1

# ---- Gravity channel ----
# Each single-channel σ is set so that channel ALONE recovers only to ~600–900 m (well above
# the ~140 m grid floor), making the fusion gain visible: the three-channel product collapses
# to ~250 m (< 500 m), no worse than the best single channel.
nmax = 3
gravity_sigma_mgal = 3.0

# ---- Magnetic channel (IGRF main field + synthetic crustal anomaly mascons, nT) ----
igrf_year = 2025.0
igrf_alt_km = 0.0
magnetic_sigma_nt = 30.0

# ---- Terrain channel (synthetic DEM) ----
dem_seed = 1
terrain_sigma_m = 40.0

# Low-degree anomalous gravity coefficients (the regional trend).
[[coeffs]]
n = 2
m = 0
cbar = 6.0e-6
sbar = 0.0

[[coeffs]]
n = 3
m = 1
cbar = 3.0e-6
sbar = 2.0e-6

# Localized gravity mascons (mGal) the track crosses.
[[mascons]]
lat_deg = 12.18
lon_deg = 20.16
amp_mgal = 45.0
sigma_deg = 0.05

[[mascons]]
lat_deg = 12.26
lon_deg = 20.22
amp_mgal = -38.0
sigma_deg = 0.045

# Synthetic crustal magnetic-anomaly mascons (nT) the track crosses.
[[magnetic_mascons]]
lat_deg = 12.20
lon_deg = 20.18
amp_mgal = 250.0
sigma_deg = 0.05

[[magnetic_mascons]]
lat_deg = 12.24
lon_deg = 20.20
amp_mgal = -200.0
sigma_deg = 0.045

scenarios.desc: Layered-PNT conflict resilience (paper P7).
scenarios.kindDesc: MODELLED layered-PNT conflict resilience (P7): a contested-environment user fields several PNT layers (open-service GNSS, wideband GNSS, an authenticated constellation, an augmentation relay), each with a base availability, a 1σ accuracy and a per-vector denial vulnerability to the shared jamming/spoofing threat. An intensity-swept SEEDED Monte-Carlo denies each layer with probability clamp(vulnerability·intensity·vector_weight,0,1), fuses the survivors by the closed-form inverse-variance rule σ_fused=(Σ 1/σ_i²)^(−1/2), and reports the total-loss probability (all layers denied), the median fused error and per-layer usable/denial statistics vs intensity. The headline resilience ratio (single-layer vs layered total-loss probability) lands at ~7x under the INDEPENDENCE assumption; a one-factor Gaussian-copula correlated-denial sweep then shows that ~7x collapse toward 1 as denial correlation rises (correlation defeats layering). A prior-sensitivity block ranges the headline over the SOURCED vulnerability priors via the mcda tornado + a Dirichlet threat-effort re-allocation + percentile CIs. VALIDATED core: the Monte-Carlo total-loss converges to the closed-form independent product Π_i p_deny_i (within MC standard error at a fixed seed and large N); the inverse-variance fuse is a closed-form identity; at ρ=0 the copula reduces to the independent model and every ρ preserves each layer's marginal denial rate. MODELLED: the per-layer vulnerability/availability/accuracy magnitudes are sourced-but-Modelled inputs (JammerTest 2024, TEXBAT, EASA SIB, RTCA DO-229, LunaNet/IOAG — see conflict_threat_params), and the specific ~7x magnitude and the ratio-vs-correlation curve shape follow from that parameterisation. A §4.2 per-vector survival breakdown then resolves the shared RF threat into the four named vectors (jamming/spoofing/kinetic/cyber) and reports each vector's usable-PNT graceful-degradation curve S_v(x)=1-Prod_i(1-a_i(1-clamp(susceptibility_i,v·x,0,1))) — VALIDATED: the seeded per-layer Monte-Carlo converges to that closed form; jamming is the sharpest vector for the correlated-RF baseline and the RF-immune inertial layer is the decisive survivor. Not a certified navigation-availability product.
scenarios.toml:
# Layered-PNT conflict resilience (paper P7).
#
# A contested-environment user fields four RF PNT layers that all ride the same band
# and therefore share the jamming/spoofing denial vector — the fragile, correlated
# case. The scenario reports:
#   * total-loss probability vs threat intensity (Monte-Carlo vs the closed-form
#     independent product it converges to),
#   * the ~7x layered-vs-single-layer resilience ratio under the independence
#     assumption,
#   * how that ~7x collapses toward 1 as the denial correlation rises (a one-factor
#     Gaussian copula) — correlation defeats layering, and
#   * a §4.2 per-vector usable-PNT survival breakdown: for each named threat vector
#     (jamming/spoofing/kinetic/cyber) acting alone, the graceful-degradation curve
#     S_v(x) = 1 - Prod_i (1 - a_i*(1 - clamp(susceptibility_i,v * x, 0, 1))). Jamming
#     is the sharpest vector for this correlated-RF stack.
#
# Every per-layer magnitude is a MODELLED input with provenance; see
# src/conflict_threat_params.rs for the sourced [min, nominal, max] priors and the
# per-vector susceptibility profiles (JammerTest 2024, TEXBAT, EASA SIB 2022-02,
# RTCA DO-229, LunaNet/IOAG). Leaving `layers` out runs the same sourced four-layer
# baseline; it is written out here — including each layer's vector_profile — for
# transparency.

kind = "conflict-resilience"
trials = 4000
seed = 20260709
primary_layer = 0

[intensity]
min = 0.0
max = 1.0
steps = 11

[correlation]
values = [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.95]

[[layers]]
name = "GNSS L1 C/A (open service)"
availability = 0.99
sigma_m = 4.0
vulnerability = 0.90
vector_weight = 0.58
# Denied at the lowest jammer power of any tracked signal; unauthenticated ⇒ spoofable.
[layers.vector_profile]
jamming = 0.98
spoofing = 0.85
kinetic = 0.12
cyber = 0.18

[[layers]]
name = "GNSS L5 / E5a (wideband)"
availability = 0.97
sigma_m = 3.0
vulnerability = 0.85
vector_weight = 0.60
# Wideband ⇒ more jam-resistant than L1 C/A but still RF-denied.
[layers.vector_profile]
jamming = 0.90
spoofing = 0.80
kinetic = 0.12
cyber = 0.18

[[layers]]
name = "Galileo E1 OS + OSNMA"
availability = 0.98
sigma_m = 4.0
vulnerability = 0.88
vector_weight = 0.59
# OSNMA authentication sharply lowers spoofing susceptibility; shared band keeps jamming high.
[layers.vector_profile]
jamming = 0.92
spoofing = 0.40
kinetic = 0.12
cyber = 0.22

[[layers]]
name = "SBAS / augmentation (WAAS/EGNOS-class)"
availability = 0.96
sigma_m = 3.0
vulnerability = 0.86
vector_weight = 0.60
# Rides the L1/L5 band (jam-fragile) and, as a networked augmentation service, carries a
# larger cyber and ground-segment kinetic surface.
[layers.vector_profile]
jamming = 0.90
spoofing = 0.68
kinetic = 0.28
cyber = 0.55

scenarios.desc: Multi-constellation coverage: the four global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) together, as a map of satellites in view, dilution of precision (DOP) and availability over the whole Earth for one day.
scenarios.kindDesc: Constellation design at scale: Walker DELTA and Walker STAR patterns in the i: T/P/F convention (nodes spread over 360 or 180 deg, in-plane spacing 360*P/T, inter-plane phase offset 360*F/T), explicit element lists and multi-shell designs, several constellations in one run, around the Earth, the Moon, Mars or any other planet, Pluto or major moon using the constants in the body module (the same ones the solar-system and body-pnt kinds use). PRESETS from published nominal elements: gps-baseline and gps-expandable (the 24 slots and the six fore/aft expandable pairs of the GPS Standard Positioning Service Performance Standard, 5th edition 2020, Tables 3.2-1 to 3.2-3), galileo (Walker 24/3/1 at 29 599.801 km and 56 deg, Galileo Open Service Service Definition Document issue 1.1 Tables 1 and 23), beidou and beidou-meo (Walker 24/3/1 at 21 528 km and 55 deg plus three geostationary satellites at 80, 110.5 and 140 deg E and three inclined geosynchronous satellites at 55 deg, BeiDou Open Service Performance Standard 3.0 section 4.1; the MEO phase and the 118 deg E inclined-geosynchronous crossing are modelled because the standard does not state them) and glonass (24/3/1 at 19 100 km and 64.8 deg from the slot formula of the GLONASS Interface Control Document edition 5.1 section 5.2). COVERAGE AND DILUTION OF PRECISION: over a latitude/longitude grid and a sampled window with an elevation mask, the number of satellites in view, GDOP, PDOP, HDOP and VDOP per cell, the availability (a fix with PDOP at or below a threshold, 6 by default) per cell, globally (area-weighted) and at the worst site, with one receiver clock per constellation unless clock = "common". It scales to thousands of satellites: visibility is a dot product against each satellite's coverage half-angle, and satellites are banded by sub-satellite latitude each epoch so a grid row tests only those that can be in view; the report counts the pair tests saved. The JSON carries the grid maps and downsampled per-satellite ground tracks. VALIDATED: the Walker generator against Galileo OS SDD Table 23 and the GLONASS ICD slot formula, the GPS preset against the published equatorial-crossing column of SPS PS Table 3.2-1, and the GPS baseline global HDOP distribution against SPS PS Appendix B (median 0.94, 95% 1.25, mean 0.96, tolerance 0.03). MODELLED: two-body orbits with optional secular J2, a spherical body, geometric visibility only (no signal power, health or terrain), and the relative phase between different systems, which is not a snapshot of any real date.
scenarios.toml:
# Multi-constellation coverage: the four global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) together,
# as a map of satellites in view, dilution of precision (DOP) and availability over the whole
# Earth for one day.
#
# Each system is a preset built from its operator's published nominal elements:
#   - GPS: the baseline 24-slot constellation, GPS Standard Positioning Service Performance
#     Standard, 5th edition (2020), Tables 3.2-1 and 3.2-3;
#   - Galileo: the Walker 24/3/1 reference constellation at 29 599.801 km semi-major axis and
#     56 deg, Galileo Open Service Service Definition Document issue 1.1, Tables 1 and 23;
#   - BeiDou: 24 medium Earth orbit satellites in a Walker 24/3/1 at 21 528 km and 55 deg,
#     3 geostationary and 3 inclined geosynchronous satellites, BeiDou Open Service
#     Performance Standard 3.0, section 4.1 (the medium-orbit phase and the inclined
#     geosynchronous crossing longitude are modelled, the standard does not state them);
#   - GLONASS: 24 satellites, 3 planes, 19 100 km, 64.8 deg, from the slot formula of the
#     GLONASS Interface Control Document edition 5.1, section 5.2.
#
# The receiver estimates one clock per system (clock = "per-constellation"), so a fix needs
# three position unknowns plus one clock for every system in view. The four systems' slot
# tables come from different reference epochs, so their relative phase is not a snapshot of
# any real date; the statistics over a day are what the run is for.
#
# What the run answers: how many satellites are in view, the position, horizontal, vertical
# and geometric DOP per 10 deg cell, and the share of time the position DOP (PDOP) is at or
# below 6 above a 10 deg mask. MODELLED: two-body orbits, a spherical Earth, geometry only.

kind = "constellation-design"
body = "earth"
duration_s = 86164.0
step_s = 900.0
mask_deg = 10.0
pdop_threshold = 6.0
grid_step_deg = 10.0
clock = "per-constellation"
track_points = 25
max_tracks = 102

[[constellation]]
name = "GPS"
preset = "gps-baseline"

[[constellation]]
name = "Galileo"
preset = "galileo"

[[constellation]]
name = "BeiDou"
preset = "beidou"

[[constellation]]
name = "GLONASS"
preset = "glonass"

scenarios.desc: Earth-GNSS reception at lunar distance.
scenarios.kindDesc: Earth-GNSS reception at lunar distance, the weak-signal layer the conflict-resilience paper names and the engine had no model for. A GNSS satellite points its antenna at the Earth; a receiver near the Moon sits about fifteen times the orbital radius away, so three things bite at once. The Earth OCCULTS THE BORESIGHT: from 26,560 km it subtends a 13.9 deg half-angle, so any lunar-bound ray must leave the transmitter at least that far off nadir, which removes the peak of the beam before any power is computed. What remains is the MAIN-LOBE EDGE AND THE SIDELOBES, the regime the LuGRE payload actually operated in during 2025. And the free-space loss is about 208 dB at L1, roughly 25 dB more than a terrestrial user pays. The report emits one row per satellite (off-boresight angle, Earth occultation, range, path loss, transmit gain at that angle, received power, carrier-to-noise density) and aggregates only the links clearing the tracking threshold. IT ALSO REPORTS THE CONDITIONING, because that is what defines this layer: every visible satellite lies inside a cone a couple of degrees wide as seen from the Moon, so the lines of sight are nearly parallel, the dilution of precision is enormous, and an Earth-GNSS fix at lunar distance is a TIMING-grade observation far more than a position-grade one. MODELLED, and the transmit pattern is the reason: the gain at angle is a uniform circular aperture (Airy), while a real GPS L1 antenna is a twelve-element helical array with a shaped main lobe and non-Airy sidelobes. Measured patterns exist and are not vendored here, so orderings and orders of magnitude are meaningful while the dB of any single satellite is not. Deliberately ABSENT, each making the budget optimistic: no ionospheric or tropospheric loss on the limb-grazing rays, no polarisation, pointing or implementation loss, and a spherical Earth with no refractive extension. The Moon position is an INPUT (range plus inertial direction) rather than an ephemeris lookup, because the quantity under test is the link and the beam geometry. Upgrading this row to Validated needs a measured transmit pattern and LuGRE normal points; neither is in the repository and neither is invented here.
scenarios.toml:
# Earth-GNSS reception at lunar distance.
#
# A GNSS constellation is built to serve users under it. A receiver near the Moon is
# roughly fifteen times the orbital radius away, outside that service volume entirely, and
# three facts decide whether it can hear anything at all:
#
#   1. THE EARTH BLOCKS THE BORESIGHT. From 26,560 km the Earth subtends a half-angle of
#      about 13.9 deg. Any ray that reaches the Moon must therefore leave the transmitter
#      at least that far off nadir — the peak of the beam is geometrically unavailable
#      before a single dB is computed.
#   2. WHAT IS LEFT IS THE EDGE OF THE MAIN LOBE AND THE SIDELOBES. The usable rays sit in
#      a thin annulus just outside the limb, where the transmit gain is already falling.
#      This is the regime the LuGRE payload operated in when it tracked GNSS at the Moon
#      in 2025.
#   3. THE PATH LOSS IS ABOUT 208 dB AT L1 — some 25 dB more than a terrestrial user pays.
#      The budget closes only with a high-gain receiving antenna, and it closes narrowly.
#
# The run reports one row per satellite (off-boresight angle, Earth occultation, range,
# path loss, transmit gain at that angle, received power, C/N0) and then aggregates only
# the links that clear the tracking threshold.
#
# READ THE CONDITIONING, NOT JUST THE COUNT
# Every satellite the receiver can hear lies inside a cone a couple of degrees wide, so the
# lines of sight are nearly parallel and the dilution of precision is enormous. That is not
# a defect of the model; it is the defining property of the layer. An Earth-GNSS fix at
# lunar distance is a TIMING-grade observation far more than a position-grade one, and the
# report prints the DOP rather than quietly omitting it.
#
# WHAT IS MODELLED, AND WHY IT IS NOT VALIDATED
# The transmit gain at angle is a uniformly illuminated circular aperture — an Airy
# pattern. A real GPS L1 antenna is a twelve-element helical array whose measured pattern
# has a shaped main lobe, deliberately peaked off-boresight to even out power across the
# Earth disc, and sidelobes that are not Airy at all. Measured patterns are published; they
# are not vendored in this repository, so they are not used here. Orderings and orders of
# magnitude are meaningful. The dB of any single satellite is not.
#
# Also absent, and every one of these makes the budget OPTIMISTIC: no ionospheric or
# tropospheric loss on the limb-grazing rays (which do clip the upper atmosphere at small
# clearance angles), no polarisation mismatch, no pointing loss, no receiver implementation
# loss, and a spherical Earth with no refractive extension of the occultation.
#
# Upgrading this to Validated needs two things the repository does not hold: a measured
# transmit pattern, and LuGRE normal points to check against. Neither is invented here.
#
# The Moon position is an INPUT — a range and an inertial direction — not an ephemeris
# lookup. What is under test is the link and the beam geometry; the engine models the lunar
# ephemeris elsewhere and coupling them would only obscure which part is being checked.

kind = "earth-gnss-lunar"

# The constellation: a 24-satellite Walker at GPS altitude and inclination.
altitude_km = 20180.0
inclination_deg = 55.0
planes = 6
sats_per_plane = 4
phasing_f = 2.0
epoch_s = 0.0

# The receiver, at the mean lunar distance along the inertial x-axis.
receiver_range_m = 384400000.0
receiver_ra_deg = 0.0
receiver_dec_deg = 0.0

# Transmitter: about 27 W into an aperture sized so the boresight gain lands near the
# 13 dBi a GPS L1 antenna is usually quoted at.
tx_power_dbw = 13.4
tx_diameter_m = 0.35
tx_efficiency = 0.6
freq_hz = 1575420000.0

# Receiver: a modest high-gain lunar antenna and a room-temperature system.
rx_gain_dbi = 12.0
system_temp_k = 290.0
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0

# Earth-observation payload footprint & coverage demonstrator (SMAD space triangle).
#
# Turns an orbit altitude + sensor field of view into the Earth angular radius,
# swath width, nadir ground sample distance, maximum off-nadir access, circular
