# The result reproduces, qualitatively, what LEO-PNT demonstrations show: the LEO carrier-to-
# noise density (C/N0) rises and falls in a bell a few minutes long, peaking several dB above
# the flat MEO (medium Earth orbit) GNSS carriers, which sit in the mid-40s to about 50 dB-Hz.
# The larger LEO signal comes from a range some forty times shorter than to a MEO satellite
# (about 26 to 32 dB less free-space loss), not from a stronger transmitter. The Galileo
# carriers use the minimum received power of the Galileo OS SIS ICD Issue 2.1 Table 12, plus
# 2 dB, scaled by range.
#
# MODELLED. No Celeste or other workshop data is used: every LEO number here comes from the
# representative preset in src/leo_link/presets/generic.rs.

# LEO-PNT end to end on a generic constellation: signal design -> pass link budget ->
# navigation message -> fused MEO + LEO fix and precise point positioning convergence.
#
# One low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) system is followed
# through every stage of the engine, with no named system's data at all:
#
# - Signal: the representative L-band design `generic-l` (binary phase-shift keying at
#   10.23 Mchip/s, pilot and data halves, 20.46 MHz transmit bandwidth) from the public
#   preset file data/leo-signals/generic-bands.toml.
# - Pass: a user in Madrid watches a designed pass of a 1080 km, 53 deg satellite peaking at
#   75 deg. The band takes the design's centre, bandwidth and chip rate and splits its
#   EIRP (equivalent isotropically radiated power) across the design's components; every
#   epoch gives the tracked (pilot) component's C/N0 (carrier-to-noise density) and its
#   band-limited code-tracking jitter.
# - Navigation message: the Galileo Keplerian set with along-track, cross-track and radial
#   correction polynomials, fitted every 300 s to a truth orbit at the pass satellite's
#   altitude and inclination; its broadcast signal-in-space range error (SISRE) is the LEO
#   orbit-and-clock error downstream.
# - Positioning: GPS and Galileo with a generic 240-satellite LEO layer (Walker 240/12/1
#   at 1080 km, 53 deg). The LEO system takes the pass's C/N0 line, the message's SISRE
#   and the design's carrier and chip rate.
# - Precise point positioning (PPP): GPS and Galileo alone and with the same LEO layer, the
#   LEO orbit-and-clock error taken from the message.
#
# MODELLED: every stage keeps its own label; the chain adds no physics.

scenarios.desc: A low-Earth-orbit positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) mega-constellation: 5 000 satellites in four Walker shells, scored as a coverage and dilution-of-precision (DOP) map.
scenarios.kindDesc: Constellation design at scale: Walker DELTA and Walker STAR patterns in the i: T/P/F convention (nodes spread over 360 or 180 deg, in-plane spacing 360*P/T, inter-plane phase offset 360*F/T), explicit element lists and multi-shell designs, several constellations in one run, around the Earth, the Moon, Mars or any other planet, Pluto or major moon using the constants in the body module (the same ones the solar-system and body-pnt kinds use). PRESETS from published nominal elements: gps-baseline and gps-expandable (the 24 slots and the six fore/aft expandable pairs of the GPS Standard Positioning Service Performance Standard, 5th edition 2020, Tables 3.2-1 to 3.2-3), galileo (Walker 24/3/1 at 29 599.801 km and 56 deg, Galileo Open Service Service Definition Document issue 1.1 Tables 1 and 23), beidou and beidou-meo (Walker 24/3/1 at 21 528 km and 55 deg plus three geostationary satellites at 80, 110.5 and 140 deg E and three inclined geosynchronous satellites at 55 deg, BeiDou Open Service Performance Standard 3.0 section 4.1; the MEO phase and the 118 deg E inclined-geosynchronous crossing are modelled because the standard does not state them) and glonass (24/3/1 at 19 100 km and 64.8 deg from the slot formula of the GLONASS Interface Control Document edition 5.1 section 5.2). COVERAGE AND DILUTION OF PRECISION: over a latitude/longitude grid and a sampled window with an elevation mask, the number of satellites in view, GDOP, PDOP, HDOP and VDOP per cell, the availability (a fix with PDOP at or below a threshold, 6 by default) per cell, globally (area-weighted) and at the worst site, with one receiver clock per constellation unless clock = "common". It scales to thousands of satellites: visibility is a dot product against each satellite's coverage half-angle, and satellites are banded by sub-satellite latitude each epoch so a grid row tests only those that can be in view; the report counts the pair tests saved. The JSON carries the grid maps and downsampled per-satellite ground tracks. VALIDATED: the Walker generator against Galileo OS SDD Table 23 and the GLONASS ICD slot formula, the GPS preset against the published equatorial-crossing column of SPS PS Table 3.2-1, and the GPS baseline global HDOP distribution against SPS PS Appendix B (median 0.94, 95% 1.25, mean 0.96, tolerance 0.03). MODELLED: two-body orbits with optional secular J2, a spherical body, geometric visibility only (no signal power, health or terrain), and the relative phase between different systems, which is not a snapshot of any real date.
scenarios.toml:
# A low-Earth-orbit positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) mega-constellation: 5 000
# satellites in four Walker shells, scored as a coverage and dilution-of-precision (DOP) map.
#
# The shells are an illustrative design, not any operator's filing:
#   - 1 600 satellites, Walker delta 1600/32/1 at 550 km and 53 deg;
#   - 1 600 satellites, Walker delta 1600/32/7 at 540 km and 53.2 deg;
#   - 1 000 satellites, Walker delta 1000/20/3 at 570 km and 70 deg;
#   -   800 satellites, Walker star 800/16/1 at 560 km and 97.6 deg (near-polar, planes
#       spread over 180 deg) to fill the high latitudes.
#
# At this size the visibility prefilter matters: each epoch the satellites are sorted by
# sub-satellite latitude and a grid row only tests those within one coverage half-angle of
# it. The `work` block of the result states how many satellite-point pair tests a brute-force
# scan would have made and how many were made. The secular J2 drift of the nodes is on, and
# the tracks are downsampled to 120 satellites.
#
# What the run answers: satellites in view, PDOP/HDOP/VDOP/GDOP per 10 deg cell, and the
# share of time with PDOP at or below 3 above a 20 deg mask over two hours. The weak spot the
# map shows is the polar caps: no shell reaches above about 82 deg latitude, so a user near a
# pole sees every satellite on one side of the sky and the vertical geometry degrades. MODELLED: an
# illustrative design, two-body orbits with J2, a spherical Earth, geometry only.

scenarios.desc: Precise point positioning (PPP) convergence with LEO augmentation.
scenarios.kindDesc: Precise point positioning (PPP) convergence with GNSS only and with LEO augmentation: a float extended Kalman filter on ionosphere-free code and carrier phase with the static station coordinates, a white receiver clock, one inter-system bias per extra system, a random-walk zenith wet delay mapped by 1/sin(elevation) and a float ambiguity per satellite arc; the precise orbit-and-clock error is white and common to the code and phase of a satellite, so each satellite is one correlated two-row update in a Joseph-stabilised form. Measurements are simulated from the same model with seeded noise over several sites and seeds, and each case (GNSS only first, then each [[case]] of LEO systems, any constellation or preset) reports the median convergence time (the first epoch after which the horizontal and vertical errors stay below the thresholds, 10 cm by default), the fraction converged, the median error curves and the filter consistency (the run-averaged position NEES against the two-sided 95% chi-square band). Optionally beside the published Li et al. (2019, J. Geod. 93:749, doi 10.1007/s00190-018-1195-2) mid-latitude figures: 9.6 min for multi-GNSS shortened to 7.0, 3.2, 2.1 and 1.3 min with 60, 96, 192 and 288 LEO satellites. MODELLED: a consistency comparison of the trend, not a reproduction of that study's constellations, noise or stations; no ambiguity resolution, cycle slips, phase wind-up, tides or time-correlated product errors.
scenarios.toml:
# Precise point positioning (PPP) convergence with LEO augmentation.
#
# A float PPP filter on ionosphere-free code and phase runs at three mid-latitude sites with
# GPS, Galileo, BeiDou (medium Earth orbit) and GLONASS, and then with each of four LEO
# constellations added. Li et al. ("LEO constellation-augmented multi-GNSS for rapid PPP
# convergence", Journal of Geodesy 93:749-764, 2019, doi 10.1007/s00190-018-1195-2) report
# multi-GNSS convergence shortened from 9.6 min to 7.0, 3.2, 2.1 and 1.3 min with 60, 96, 192
# and 288 LEO satellites; `compare_li_2019` puts those figures beside the modelled ones.
#
# The four LEO constellations here are representative Walker delta shells at 1000 km and
# 60 deg with 60, 96, 192 and 288 satellites; they are NOT the paper's designs, and the noise,
# stations and convergence definition (horizontal and vertical errors below 10 cm until the
# end of the run) are this model's. The comparison is therefore a MODELLED consistency check
# on the trend: convergence must shorten monotonically with the number of LEO satellites.
kind = "leo-ppp"
seed = 20
duration_s = 1800.0
step_s = 10.0

scenarios.desc: LEO-PNT resilience mission: GNSS jammed, LEO-PNT carries the user, integrity maintained.
scenarios.kindDesc: Campaign: existing scenario kinds composed into one run, with every number read from a real run of the named kind. Four sections, in any combination. PHASES: a chained mission on one shared timeline -- each phase runs one or more scenarios (for example jamming, then spoofing, then a clock in holdover with an inertial navigation system coasting beside it, then an integrity alarm, then recovery), their outputs are read into named channels (clock time error against its guard, carrier-to-noise density ratio against the tracking floor, protection level against the alert limit, position error, satellites tracking, alarm flags) by a per-kind preset or by explicit result paths, and resampled onto a common grid by zero-order hold, with phase boundaries and events; state is handed on by carry (a channel continues from the previous phase's end value), handoff (a previous phase's number written into this phase's scenario) and end_at (a phase ends at a time a run computed, such as a spoofing monitor's detection time). SWEEP: a grid over one to three dotted scenario keys of any kind (a whole-number segment indexes an array of tables, as in system.2.sisre_m), with metrics read by result path and, with runs above one, a seeded Monte Carlo ensemble at every node. MONTE_CARLO: realisation k runs at base_seed + k; each metric reports mean, standard deviation, nearest-rank 5th/50th/95th percentiles and a fixed-seed bootstrap 95% confidence interval on the mean. COMPOSE: several scenarios under shared values (one jammer's power and position written into a maritime and a road receiver), with a combined best/worst summary. The result carries a campaign hash, a digest over every member result, and a units entry for every emitted number; the interoperability exports write each member scenario that has geometry as its own file set. Composition identities are tested: a one-phase campaign reproduces the stand-alone run bit for bit, a fixed-seed ensemble is byte-stable, and on a white-frequency-noise clock the ensemble mean falls inside the reported interval with the spread matching sqrt(q_wf * tau). MODELLED: the additive carry and the zero-order hold are modelling choices, and each phase carries the label of the kind that ran it.
scenarios.toml:
# LEO-PNT resilience mission: GNSS jammed, LEO-PNT carries the user, integrity maintained.
#
# Three phases on one 30 s timeline, each running a `spectrum` receiver (what it can still
# track) and an `integrity` run (receiver autonomous integrity monitoring, RAIM, against a
# 40 m horizontal and 50 m vertical alert limit):
#
#   nominal   GPS L1 C/A, Galileo E5a and a generic low Earth orbit (LEO) positioning,
#             navigation and timing (PNT) layer in the S and C bands all track; integrity
#             uses the GNSS layer (24 satellites at 20 200 km) and the LEO layer (240 at
#             1080 km, 53 deg, and 72 at 1080 km, 97 deg) together.
#   jammed    two barrage jammers, one over L1 and one over L5/E5, at -95 dBW received:
#             both GNSS signals fall below the 25 dB-Hz tracking floor; the S- and C-band
#             LEO signals are untouched. Integrity runs on the LEO layer alone.
#   recovery  the jammers stop; both layers again.
#
# The alarm channel is the integrity kind's own: raised at epochs where the protection
# level cannot be formed or exceeds the alert limit. With GNSS jammed the LEO layer alone
# still forms a protection level at every epoch; it is under the 50 m alert limit at 28
# of the 30 grid times and the alarm is raised at the other two. That is integrity
# working: the user is warned whenever the bound is too large, and availability, not
# integrity, is what the jamming costs.
#
# The integrity runs use that kind's own user track (a circular track 0.4 km up, the
# convention of the other bundled integrity runs), not the spectrum receiver's site, and
# a 1 m user-equivalent range error for both layers; those are scenario choices, stated
# here. The integrity kind does not see the jammer: the jammed phase's LEO-only
# constellation is the campaign's statement of what the spectrum run says is left.
# MODELLED.
kind = "campaign"
title = "GNSS jammed, LEO-PNT carries the user, integrity maintained"

scenarios.desc: LEO-PNT resilience from received power: the jammer-to-signal (J/S) margin.
scenarios.kindDesc: L-band spectrum model and waterfall: the whole GNSS L band as one power spectral density (PSD), frequency across, time down, over a scripted jammer timeline. SIGNALS: GPS L1 C/A and L2C (BPSK(1)), Galileo E1 open service (MBOC(6,1,1/11), or BOC(1,1)), GPS L5 and Galileo E5a (BPSK(10)), each at its carrier with the interface-specification minimum received power (IS-GPS-200, IS-GPS-705, Galileo OS SIS ICD) unless overridden; GLONASS, BeiDou and Galileo E6 are not modelled. JAMMERS: continuous-wave tone, flat narrowband noise, linear sawtooth chirp and broadband noise matched to a band's own modulation, each with a centre, a bandwidth, a received power (direct, or EIRP and range through the jamming kind's free-space path loss) and on/off times. Each jammer is scored against each band by its spectral separation coefficient kappa over the receiver bandwidth, and (C/N0)_eff = [1/(C/N0) + sum (J/S) kappa]^-1; for one jammer this equals the jamming kind's anti-jam equation with Q = 1/(R_c kappa), and the report carries that cross-check (and the jamming kind's representative-Q figure beside it). The noise floor is k T_sys with T_sys = T_ant + 290 K (F - 1). The waterfall averages each cell over its bin and its row (chirps exactly, whole sweeps plus the partial one; jammers switching mid-row by their duty), so the C/N0 timeline and the picture come from the same numbers; result.json carries the grid block-averaged in power, per-band C/N0 and J/S per row, and per jammer per band the SSC, Q, J/S, in-band J/S and steady C/N0. Optional [iq]: the model drawn as complex IQ at one instant, written to and read back from a SigMF recording (cf32_le or ci16_le), and compared with a Welch estimate. Optional [recording] (native builds): a real SigMF recording's Welch PSD beside the model. VALIDATED: the signal PSDs against the textbook main-lobe widths (BPSK(n) 2n x 1.023 MHz null to null; BOC(1,1) lobes centred at +/-1.023 MHz) and the spectral separation coefficients against their Parseval closed forms and Kaplan & Hegarty's Q = 1 (CW) and 1.5 (matched). MODELLED: jammer powers, timeline, front-end bandwidths, the continuous-spectrum (no code lines) treatment and the absence of AGC, blanking and antenna pattern.
scenarios.toml:
# LEO-PNT resilience from received power: the jammer-to-signal (J/S) margin.
#
# A jammer denies a signal when the jammer power it lets through, relative to the signal's
# own received power, pushes the effective carrier-to-noise density (C/N0) below the
# tracking threshold. A low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite is about 20 to 40 times closer than
# a medium Earth orbit (MEO) GNSS satellite, so the same transmitter delivers 26 to 32 dB
# more power, and every dB of received power is a dB of J/S margin.
#
# One wideband (barrage) noise jammer, 40 MHz wide at 1185 MHz, covers GPS L5, Galileo E5a
# and two LEO signals in the same band. Its received power steps up by 5 dB every 10 s
# from -125 dBW at 10 s to -90 dBW at 80 s. The `spectrum` kind's first-loss time of
# each band is where the jammer takes it:
#   gps-l5       interface-document minimum, -157.9 dBW
#   galileo-e5a  interface-document minimum, -155.0 dBW
#   xona-x5      the published minimum received power, -144.9 dBW (arXiv 2509.19551)
#   generic-l    a representative LEO L-band signal at -135 dBW, 1191.795 MHz
# GPS L5 is lost at the -105 dBW step, Galileo E5a at -100 dBW, Xona X5 at -95 dBW; the
# generic signal still tracks at -90 dBW. Received power buys J/S margin dB for dB.
# Received powers are those at the stated minimum; a real pass varies over it (see the
# leo-pass scenarios).
#
# MODELLED: the signal spectra are validated closed forms; the jammer steps and the
# received powers are scenario inputs.
kind = "spectrum"
seed = 12
duration_s = 100.0
step_s = 1.0

[receiver]
noise_figure_db = 2.0
antenna_temp_k = 290.0
tracking_threshold_dbhz = 25.0

scenarios.kindDesc: LEO pass and link budget, band by band, for LEO-PNT (positioning, navigation and timing from low Earth orbit), system-agnostic: a user (ground, maritime, air or indoor, static or moving) and one or more LEO satellites from a DESIGNED PASS (a circular orbit placed so the user sees one pass of a chosen maximum elevation at a chosen time, sun-synchronous if asked), explicit ELEMENTS, a TLE (two-line element set) through the engine's SGP4, or a WALKER constellation built by the constellation-design code (the highest passes reported). Bands come from a named preset (generic multi-band UHF/L/S/C, generic C band, Xona Pulsar X1/X5, Iridium STL, Starlink as a Doppler-only signal of opportunity, CentiSpace, and an optional Celeste IOD preset marked WORKSHOP) or are written into the scenario; each preset states whether its numbers are PUBLIC (with URL), REPRESENTATIVE or WORKSHOP. Per satellite, band and epoch: elevation, azimuth, range, range rate and range acceleration; free-space path loss; EIRP and the satellite pattern gain (isoflux, Gaussian beam or flat); user antenna gain against elevation (patch, hemispherical or isotropic); gaseous attenuation (ITU-R P.676-10 Annex 2), rain attenuation (ITU-R P.838-3 coefficients and the P.618-14 procedure, from a rain rate and rain height), tropospheric scintillation (ITU-R P.618-14 section 2.4.1), building entry loss for an indoor user (ITU-R P.2109-2), polarisation mismatch, system noise temperature and C/N0 (carrier-to-noise density); Doppler and Doppler rate in closed form from the range rate and range acceleration, each checked against central differences; the first-order ionospheric delay 40.3 STEC/f^2 from a Klobuchar or vertical-TEC slant TEC scaled to the part of the ionosphere below the satellite. Band pairs get the ionosphere-free coefficients, noise amplification and code noise at the pass peak. MEO GNSS satellites (Galileo or GPS presets) are evaluated with the same antenna and noise model from their interface-document received powers, so the LEO bell-shaped pass and the flat GNSS carriers share one plot. An optional [iot] section gives time to first fix, energy per fix and battery life against duty cycle for a stated receiver power budget (MODELLED). Each band pair also gives the slant TEC its geometry-free combination recovers at the peak and that estimate's code-noise sigma (ionosphere sounding). An optional [spoofer] section counterfeits the signals of a claimed position that jumps or is pushed from the true one after an onset and runs two monitors with stated false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities: Doppler and pass-geometry consistency (measured range rates against those predicted from the orbits and an independent prior position and velocity, a generalised least-squares chi-square test over a window, on the GNSS, LEO and all channels) and cross-band consistency (the epoch-to-epoch step of each LEO band pair's model-corrected geometry-free combination), reporting per-epoch statistics and when each monitor detects (MODELLED). VALIDATED components: free-space loss, the P.838-3 coefficients against its Table 5, the P.618-14 rain and scintillation procedures and the P.2109 building entry loss against the ITU-R Study Group 3 validation examples, the IS-GPS-200 L1/L2 group-delay ratio, and the static-user maximum Doppler of a circular orbit against arXiv 2509.19551 Table 1. MODELLED: EIRPs, patterns, the Chapman fraction of TEC below the satellite and the whole pass.
scenarios.toml:
# LEO-PNT resilience against spoofing: Doppler and pass-geometry consistency.
#
# A timing receiver at a surveyed site (Frankfurt, position known to 1 m, velocity known
# to be zero within 2 mm/s) tracks Galileo E1 and a generic low Earth orbit (LEO)
# positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) layer (240 satellites at 1080 km, 53 deg; the
# 16 highest passes of the half hour). At 300 s a spoofer captures every channel and
# presents a position 30 m east of the true one, self-consistently in range and range
# rate: the counterfeit signals are what a receiver 30 m away would see, the ionospheric
# delay included (so the cross-band monitor has nothing to see; `leo-resilience-spoof-
# monitors` shows the spoofers it does catch).
#
# The receiver predicts each satellite's range rate from the broadcast orbit and its
# surveyed position and tests the measured range rates (chi-square, false-alarm
# probability 1e-5 per epoch, detection declared at 99.9 % probability). A 30 m error
# changes a MEO GNSS range rate by about 4 mm/s, inside the frequency-lock-loop noise;
# it changes a LEO range rate by about 10 cm/s, because a LEO satellite's transverse
# velocity over its range is about 25 times larger. The GNSS-only test never sees the
# spoofer; the test on every channel (GNSS and LEO, sharing one receiver clock drift, which
# the GNSS channels pin) detects it once enough LEO satellites are in view, 105 s after
# the onset.
#
# MODELLED: the monitor's statistics are exact for the stated Gaussian noise; the spoofer
# is an idealised position jump (its power, angle of arrival and correlation-peak
# signatures are not modelled), and the prior is independent of the spoofed fixes.
kind = "leo-pass"
name = "Spoofing detection by LEO Doppler consistency"
epoch = "2026-09-28T08:00:00"
duration_s = 1800.0
step_s = 5.0

lat_deg = 50.11
lon_deg = 8.68

[[leo_constellation.design.shell]]
total = 240
planes = 12
phasing = 1
altitude_km = 1080.0
inclination_deg = 53.0

[gnss]

simulate_iono = true
prior_sigma_m = 1.0

scenarios.desc: Time transfer to UTC from LEO satellites, against C/N0 and the receiver oscillator.
scenarios.kindDesc: Fused medium-Earth-orbit (MEO) and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) over ANY constellations: each [[system]] is a GNSS preset of the constellation-design kind, a LEO preset (xona-pulsar, iridium-stl, starlink-sop, centispace, generic-c-band, the atomic-zero-clock ephemeris model, or another preset file, each in its own file with its sources marked PUBLIC, WORKSHOP or DERIVED), Walker shells or explicit element sets, with a carrier, a chip rate, a carrier-to-noise density (C/N0) envelope from the elevation mask to the zenith, a signal-in-space range error (SISRE), a Doppler sigma and a clock model (its own receiver clock, so the inter-system bias is estimated, or a known broadcast offset). Four modes. DOPPLER: batch Gauss-Newton positioning from range rate with analytic partials, clock-drift and optional velocity states and an optional height constraint, single- or multi-satellite, the error against window length, the Doppler, Doppler-rate and jerk envelope of each LEO system, and the single-pass along-track and cross-track accuracy against the cross-track offset (the cross-track error grows without bound as the pass goes overhead; a single pass also has a mirror solution across the ground track). A Doppler-only signal of opportunity (starlink-sop) runs here. JOINT: per-epoch weighted least-squares pseudorange fixes from GNSS alone, LEO alone and both, per-measurement sigmas from a delay-lock-loop thermal-noise model at C/N0 plus the SISRE (or a fixed sigma, so a signal model can feed them), the estimated inter-system biases, and PDOP/HDOP/VDOP against the number of LEO satellites added. POLAR: satellites in view and DOP against latitude for GNSS, LEO and both. TIMING: time transfer to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) from LEO satellites at a known position with a two-state clock filter whose process noise comes from the engine's oscillator classes, against C/N0 and the oscillator, and the IS-GPS-200 system-time-to-UTC expression; with [timing] trace = true every row also reports its time error and predicted sigma at every epoch. VALIDATED: the largest Doppler of an overhead-to-horizon pass against the published Iridium (up to 36 kHz) and Xona Pulsar X1 (32 to 34 kHz) figures. MODELLED: everything else; the DOP is checked against a hand-derived case, the fixes against their covariance, and the Doppler model against the range-acceleration identity.
scenarios.toml:
# Time transfer to UTC from LEO satellites, against C/N0 and the receiver oscillator.
#
# A timing receiver at a surveyed site in Boulder, Colorado recovers its clock from the
# Iridium constellation (the `iridium-stl` preset: 66 satellites at 780 km, L-band bursts,
# received power 300 to 2400 times GPS), holds time with its own oscillator when no
# satellite is in view, and converts the system time to UTC with the broadcast offset
# (IS-GPS-200 expression; the parameters below are illustrative, with a 5 ns uncertainty).
# Four oscillator classes (TCXO, OCXO, chip-scale atomic clock, rubidium) and four C/N0
# offsets are compared over six hours, every row with the same seed so the rows differ only
# in C/N0 and oscillator. The Iridium bursts arrive 25 to 34 dB above GPS, so the loop noise
# of the 25 000 symbol/s ranging signal matters only when the C/N0 is cut by 20 dB or more;
# at nominal power the 5 m representative signal-in-space range error and the UTC-offset
# uncertainty set the floor, and with a satellite in view about 93% of the time the
# oscillator matters little.
#
# NIST measured Iridium PNT timing receivers with a miniature atomic clock within 40 ns of
# UTC(NIST) over 40 days (https://www.nist.gov/publications/validating-timing-performance-improvement-ionospheric-corrections-iridium-pnt-receivers).
# The modelled figures are a consistency comparison with that, not a reproduction of the test.
# `trace = true` adds each row's time error at every epoch, so the run animates
# (`--animate html`); the row statistics are the same with or without it.
# MODELLED.
kind = "leo-pvt"
mode = "timing"
seed = 9
duration_s = 21600.0

scenarios.kindDesc: Campaign: existing scenario kinds composed into one run, with every number read from a real run of the named kind. Four sections, in any combination. PHASES: a chained mission on one shared timeline -- each phase runs one or more scenarios (for example jamming, then spoofing, then a clock in holdover with an inertial navigation system coasting beside it, then an integrity alarm, then recovery), their outputs are read into named channels (clock time error against its guard, carrier-to-noise density ratio against the tracking floor, protection level against the alert limit, position error, satellites tracking, alarm flags) by a per-kind preset or by explicit result paths, and resampled onto a common grid by zero-order hold, with phase boundaries and events; state is handed on by carry (a channel continues from the previous phase's end value), handoff (a previous phase's number written into this phase's scenario) and end_at (a phase ends at a time a run computed, such as a spoofing monitor's detection time). SWEEP: a grid over one to three dotted scenario keys of any kind (a whole-number segment indexes an array of tables, as in system.2.sisre_m), with metrics read by result path and, with runs above one, a seeded Monte Carlo ensemble at every node. MONTE_CARLO: realisation k runs at base_seed + k; each metric reports mean, standard deviation, nearest-rank 5th/50th/95th percentiles and a fixed-seed bootstrap 95% confidence interval on the mean. COMPOSE: several scenarios under shared values (one jammer's power and position written into a maritime and a road receiver), with a combined best/worst summary. The result carries a campaign hash, a digest over every member result, and a units entry for every emitted number; the interoperability exports write each member scenario that has geometry as its own file set. Composition identities are tested: a one-phase campaign reproduces the stand-alone run bit for bit, a fixed-seed ensemble is byte-stable, and on a white-frequency-noise clock the ensemble mean falls inside the reported interval with the spread matching sqrt(q_wf * tau). scenarios.toml:
# LEO-PNT vertical: wireless networks, 5G/6G base-station timing.
#
# A 5G time-division-duplex (TDD) base station in Madrid needs its time within 1.5
# microseconds of every other cell's (ITU-T G.8271 accuracy class 4 at the end
# application; 1.1 microseconds at the network reference point, G.8271.1). Its
# oven-controlled crystal oscillator (OCXO) is disciplined to GNSS. When GNSS is lost for
# a day:
#
#   * the `telecom-timing` kind runs the operator's own holdover analysis of the OCXO
#     (temperature cycling of 2 K, the kind's G.8271.1 and G.8272 budgets): the events mark
#     when its time error crosses the 1100 ns network limit and the 1500 ns end-application
#     limit;
#   * a `leo-pvt` timing run disciplines the same class of oscillator to the Xona Pulsar X5
#     signal (public signal table, arXiv 2509.19551; both published shells, 258 satellites
#     at about 1080 km) and converts system time to UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) with
#     the broadcast offset, holding between passes;
#   * a `leo-pass` run of the four highest Pulsar passes over the site carries the geometry
#     the campaign exports.
#
# The alarm is raised on the LEO-disciplined time error against the 1100 ns network limit.
#
# MODELLED: the two oscillator models are each kind's own (the telecom kind's OCXO with
# temperature and ageing terms, the timing run's OCXO class noise), so the comparison is
# between the two analyses, not one oscillator; the X5 range error is the preset's.

title = "5G base-station timing: holdover and LEO time"

# LEO-PNT vertical: autonomous vehicles, an urban canyon with a LEO layer.
#
# A car drives east through Munich. On the open road every satellite above 10 deg is

# a `leo-pvt` joint fix (GPS, Galileo and a generic low Earth orbit (LEO) layer of 240
# satellites at 1080 km, 53 deg, with a 0.25 m signal-in-space range error), comparing the
# GNSS-only error with the fused GNSS + LEO error against a 1.5 m lane-level threshold,
# and a `leo-pass` run of one LEO pass seen from the moving car (its geometry is what the
# campaign exports).
#

# threshold at about half the canyon epochs, where the alarm is raised.

# `automotive-urban-canyon` scenario covers the inertial side of the same drive.

scenarios.kindDesc: Campaign: existing scenario kinds composed into one run, with every number read from a real run of the named kind. Four sections, in any combination. PHASES: a chained mission on one shared timeline -- each phase runs one or more scenarios (for example jamming, then spoofing, then a clock in holdover with an inertial navigation system coasting beside it, then an integrity alarm, then recovery), their outputs are read into named channels (clock time error against its guard, carrier-to-noise density ratio against the tracking floor, protection level against the alert limit, position error, satellites tracking, alarm flags) by a per-kind preset or by explicit result paths, and resampled onto a common grid by zero-order hold, with phase boundaries and events; state is handed on by carry (a channel continues from the previous phase's end value), handoff (a previous phase's number written into this phase's scenario) and end_at (a phase ends at a time a run computed, such as a spoofing monitor's detection time). SWEEP: a grid over one to three dotted scenario keys of any kind (a whole-number segment indexes an array of tables, as in system.2.sisre_m), with metrics read by result path and, with runs above one, a seeded Monte Carlo ensemble at every node. MONTE_CARLO: realisation k runs at base_seed + k; each metric reports mean, standard deviation, nearest-rank 5th/50th/95th percentiles and a fixed-seed bootstrap 95% confidence interval on the mean. COMPOSE: several scenarios under shared values (one jammer's power and position written into a maritime and a road receiver), with a combined best/worst summary. The result carries a campaign hash, a digest over every member result, and a units entry for every emitted number; the interoperability exports write each member scenario that has geometry as its own file set. Composition identities are tested: a one-phase campaign reproduces the stand-alone run bit for bit, a fixed-seed ensemble is byte-stable, and on a white-frequency-noise clock the ensemble mean falls inside the reported interval with the spread matching sqrt(q_wf * tau). MODELLED: the additive carry and the zero-order hold are modelling choices, and each phase carries the label of the kind that ran it.
scenarios.toml:
# LEO-PNT vertical: critical infrastructure timing, holdover with LEO time.
#
# A grid-edge time server at a substation in Boulder, Colorado must hold the 1 microsecond
# synchronisation that power-system protection and phasor measurement need (the IEC/IEEE
# 61850-9-3 power profile). Its oscillator is a temperature-compensated crystal (TCXO)
# class part, disciplined to GNSS. When GNSS is lost:
#
#   gnss-locked  (10 min) the `clock` kind's TCXO tracks GNSS: time error near zero.
#   gnss-denied  (24 h) the same TCXO coasts on its own: its random-walk frequency noise
#                makes the time error grow as t^1.5, through the 1000 ns guard a little
#                over an hour after the loss and to about 29 microseconds by the end of
#                the day. Beside it, a `leo-pvt` timing run disciplines the same TCXO class
#                to the Iridium constellation (the public `iridium-stl` preset: 66
#                satellites at 780 km, L-band bursts 25 to 34 dB above GPS), holding
#                between passes, and converts system time to UTC (Coordinated Universal
#                Time) with the broadcast offset. A `leo-pass` run of one Iridium pass over
#                the site carries the geometry the campaign exports.
#
# The alarm is raised on the LEO-disciplined time error against the 1000 ns guard; it
# stays down. The free-running error is shown for comparison and is not alarmed. Both
# runs use the same oscillator noise (the engine's TCXO class); the deterministic
# frequency offset and ageing are taken as calibrated at the loss of GNSS.
#
# NIST measured Iridium PNT timing receivers with a miniature atomic clock within 40 ns of
# UTC(NIST) over 40 days (https://www.nist.gov/publications/validating-timing-performance-improvement-ionospheric-corrections-iridium-pnt-receivers);
# the modelled figures are a consistency comparison with that, not a reproduction.
# MODELLED.
kind = "campaign"
title = "Critical infrastructure timing: holdover with LEO time"

# LEO-PNT vertical: polar and Arctic users.
#
# GNSS medium Earth orbit (MEO) planes are inclined 55 to 56 deg, so from the Arctic every
# GNSS satellite sits in the southern half of the sky at low elevation, and the vertical
# geometry suffers. A polar low Earth orbit (LEO) constellation passes overhead there
# most often. A user travels north through three phases of an hour each, Tromso (69.7 N),
# Longyearbyen on Svalbard (78.2 N) and the North Pole drift ice (89.5 N); each phase runs
# a `leo-pvt` joint fix of GPS and Galileo, with and without the Iridium constellation (the

# 5 m signal-in-space range error), and a `leo-pass` run of the three highest Iridium
# passes of a quarter hour over the site, whose geometry the campaign exports.
#
# Channels: the GNSS-only and fused 3D errors, their position dilution of precision
# (PDOP) and the satellites in view. The alarm is raised where the fused error exceeds
# 3 m. `polar-arctic-leo-coverage` gives the same comparison as a table over latitude.
#
# MODELLED: two-body orbits with J2 from each constellation preset; no ionospheric
# scintillation, which the auroral zone would add.

# LEO-PNT vertical: railway and maritime, the bundled maritime and rail scenarios plus LEO.

#                  in its S and C bands, which the L1 jammer does not reach.
#   rail-tunnel    `rail-tunnel-coast` (a train at 44.4 m/s coasting on a tactical inertial
#                  unit in a tunnel, no aiding): the event marks the moment its position
#                  error reaches 2 m, the kind's own crossing time.
#   rail-open      back in the open, a `leo-pass` run of the train (160 km/h east of
#                  Hamburg) tracks a generic LEO satellite (1080 km, 97 deg) in its L
#                  and S bands, the signals a re-acquiring receiver would use to end
#                  the coast.
#
# The alarm follows the jamming kind's own rule (fewer than four GNSS satellites
# tracking) in the strait. The jamming and LEO runs do not share a model: the leo-pass kind
# has no jammer, and the S and C bands are outside the L1 jammer's 20 MHz by construction.
# MODELLED.

scenarios.desc: One-way link budget demonstrator (comms & link budgets, trade-study tier).
scenarios.kindDesc: One-way link budget over the CCSDS 401 / DSN 810-005 link equation: free-space path loss, C/N₀, Eb/N₀, margin and closure for a transmit EIRP, receive G/T, range, data rate and band (s|x|ka) against a required Eb/N₀. A deterministic engineering calculation from the supplied inputs (not a calibrated terminal datasheet).
scenarios.toml:
# One-way link budget demonstrator (comms & link budgets, trade-study tier).
#
# Applies the CCSDS 401 / DSN 810-005 link equation
#   C/N0 = EIRP - FSPL - L_other + G/T - k ;  Eb/N0 = C/N0 - 10log10(R_b)
# and reports free-space path loss, C/N0, Eb/N0, margin and whether the link closes
# against a required Eb/N0.
#
# HONEST SCOPE: a deterministic engineering calculation from the supplied inputs
# (EIRP / G/T / range / rate / losses) -- NOT a calibrated terminal datasheet.
# Run:  kshana scenarios/link-budget.toml
kind = "link-budget"

band = "x"                  # s | x | ka (sets the free-space-loss frequency)
eirp_dbw = 55.0
g_over_t_db = 53.0
range_km = 2000.0
data_rate_bps = 1.0e6
other_losses_db = 3.0
required_eb_n0_db = 4.5

# Optional: the receive system noise temperature (K). It is NOT an input to the link
# equation -- that needs only the ratio G/T -- but stating it lets the report also give
# the receive antenna gain the figure of merit implies (G = G/T + 10*log10(T_sys)).
# Left out, the gain split is absent from the report rather than assumed.
# tsys_k = 300.0

scenarios.desc: Lunar south-pole integrity: an Artemis-region landed receiver against a representative LunaNet relay set, ARAIM protection levels over a 24 h pass.
scenarios.kindDesc: Lunar south-pole ARAIM protection-level pass vs a representative LunaNet relay set. sigma_ure_m exposes the signal-in-space ranging accuracy (protection levels scale linearly with it, so sweeping it answers what ranging accuracy an alert limit requires). Defaults to the historical LNIS-class south-pole case.
scenarios.toml:
# Lunar south-pole integrity: an Artemis-region landed receiver against a
# representative LunaNet relay set, ARAIM protection levels over a 24 h pass.
#
# The lunar navigation signal is far weaker and the relay constellation far sparser
# than GPS (LunaNet LNIS: σ_URE ≈ 30 m vs GPS ≈ 0.6 m), and the protection level
# scales linearly with σ_URE — so this honestly surfaces the integrity gap: with
# 30 m ranging the HPL is finite but exceeds a 50 m surface-ops alert limit, i.e. the
# surface user is not yet "available". This is the quantitative statement that lunar
# PNT integrity is hard, not a claim that it is met.
#
# Scope: a representative selenocentric relay sky (src/lunar.rs south_pole_hpl_pass),
# not the precise differential-corrected 9:2 LANS NRHO — the CR3BP three-body core is
# in src/cr3bp.rs; wiring real NRHO relay ephemerides + DE421 libration are follow-ons.
kind = "lunar-integrity"

step_s = 3600.0        # 1 h samples
duration_s = 86400.0   # 24 h pass
alert_limit_m = 50.0   # LunaNet surface-ops alert limit
p_hmi = 1.0e-4         # lunar surface integrity-risk budget (not aviation 1e-7)

scenarios.desc: Lunar surface-navigation signal-security attack surface (paper P1).
scenarios.kindDesc: Lunar surface-navigation signal-security attack surface (P1): composes the open signal-security analyses into one binary-reachable run. Reports (1) the AFS received power and its power SURPLUS versus a terrestrial GPS reference, plus the 12-18 dB sensitivity band as a genuine multi-axis sweep over the link inputs (reference level x EIRP x slant range) with the 25x-rounded / 28x-unrounded linear-factor reconciliation. REVISED (rule R4): this reported a 15.6 dB power DEFICIT and a 32x/36x factor until the GPS reference was corrected from -125 / -128.5 (which are the dBm figures) to -155 / -158.5 dBW, the ICD-GPS-200 values the jamming module has always carried. The sign inverts: the modelled lunar AFS signal is 14.4 dB STRONGER than terrestrial GPS L1 C/A, not weaker. The received power itself did not move by a bit, and the linear factor is the old one over exactly 1000, which is exactly the 30 dB dBm-to-dBW offset; (2) the required attacker transmit power to spoof (J/S = 3 dB) and to deny (J/S = 30 dB) at each standoff, the inverse of the J/S link; (3) the orbital capture footprint under a real uniform-aperture antenna pattern (Airy [2 J1(x)/x]^2), an altitude-limited sub-hemispheric cap whose limb is NOT captured; (4) a computed tracking-loop spoof-capture pull-in outcome (does a matched-code spoofer at a given power advantage and code offset actually drag the DLL/PLL) rather than the asserted 3 dB threshold; (5) the airless-body geometric horizon reach of a raised surface transmitter; and (6) the OSNMA/TESLA authentication budget (20 bit/s overhead = ~40 % of a 50 bit/s AFS nav message, key-disclosure latency, 2^-40 forgery). An empty body reproduces the P1 baseline; every input is defaulted and overridable. VALIDATED sub-results carry their source module's oracle (closed-form dB radiometry; inverse-J/S round trip; Airy pattern vs A&S Bessel and spherical-cap geometry; DLL/PLL pull-in vs Kaplan & Hegarty; spherical-tangent horizon identity vs eo_payload; OSNMA SIS-ICD field sizing). MODELLED: the representative geometry/power magnitudes and the specific capture-map cell values. Not a certified security product.
scenarios.toml:
# Lunar surface-navigation signal-security attack surface (paper P1).
#
# Composes the open signal-security analyses into one binary-reachable run:
#   * link-budget power deficit vs a terrestrial GPS reference + the 12-18 dB
#     sensitivity band (a genuine reference x EIRP x slant-range sweep) with the
#     32x-rounded / 36x-unrounded linear-factor reconciliation,
#   * the attacker transmit power required to spoof (J/S = 3 dB) and to deny
#     (J/S = 30 dB) at each standoff (the inverse of the J/S link),
#   * the orbital capture footprint under a real uniform-aperture antenna pattern
#     (an altitude-limited sub-hemispheric cap whose limb is NOT captured),
#   * a computed tracking-loop spoof-capture pull-in outcome (does a matched-code
#     spoofer at +6 dB / 0.3-chip actually drag the DLL/PLL) rather than the
#     asserted 3 dB threshold,
#   * the airless-body geometric horizon reach of a raised surface transmitter, and
#   * the OSNMA/TESLA authentication budget (20 bit/s = ~40 % of a 50 bit/s AFS nav
#     message, key-disclosure latency, 2^-40 forgery).
#
# Every input is defaulted to the P1 baseline; the body below leaves them at their
# defaults (so this reproduces the paper's headline figures) while naming the knobs.
# Override any field to explore a different attacker / link geometry.

kind = "lunar-attack-surface"

# Link geometry (defaults shown for transparency).
afs_eirp_dbw = 26.0
user_gain_dbi = 3.0
slant_range_m = 3.0e6
carrier_hz = 2.4e9
gps_reference_dbw = -155.0       # GPS L1 C/A typical received power, dBW (was -125.0, which is dBm)
gps_reference_min_dbw = -158.5   # ICD-GPS-200 specification minimum, dBW (was -128.5, which is dBm)

# Orbital transmitter + footprint.
transmitter_altitude_m = 100_000.0
antenna_diameter_m = 1.0
footprint_grid = 400

# Attacker standoffs (m) for the required-transmit-power curve.
standoffs_m = [1_000.0, 10_000.0, 100_000.0]

# Representative spoofer for the tracking-loop pull-in.
spoof_power_advantage_db = 6.0
spoof_code_offset_chips = 0.3

# Capture-footprint sweep axes: the captured fraction above is ONE operating point
# (100 km, 1 m dish); these sweep it over transmitter altitude x beamwidth so the
# fraction is read against the two inputs that set it, and so limb capture is reported
# as a threshold (the altitude / beamwidth / transmit power at which it switches on)
# rather than a boolean at a single point. Both defaults are chosen so the baseline
# operating point above is an exact sample of the grid.
footprint_altitude_min_m = 20_000.0    # 20 km ... 500 km in 80 km steps
footprint_altitude_max_m = 500_000.0
footprint_altitude_steps = 7
footprint_altitude_scale = "linear"
footprint_diameter_min_m = 0.25        # 0.25 m ... 4 m, i.e. HPBW 29.2 deg ... 1.83 deg
footprint_diameter_max_m = 4.0
footprint_diameter_steps = 5
footprint_diameter_scale = "log"

scenarios.desc: Surface-beacon augmentation of a lunar orbital navigation service.
scenarios.kindDesc: Surface-beacon augmentation of a lunar orbital navigation service, as a runnable before/after table. A south-polar user sees a sparse orbital set in a narrow patch of sky, so the ranging geometry is ill-conditioned; a few SURVEYED SURFACE BEACONS supply the low-elevation, wide-azimuth line-of-sight rows an all-overhead set lacks, and the horizontal dilution of precision collapses. The scenario reports three configurations at one epoch — satellites alone, satellites plus the visible beacons, and a larger constellation as the alternative route to the same geometry — each with its visible-source counts, its full DOP, and the realised 1-sigma accuracy in METRES obtained by multiplying through a per-beacon user-equivalent ranging error assembled as the root-sum-square of clock-synchronisation, multipath and survey terms. Beacon visibility is the airless-Moon two-height geometric horizon (no atmosphere, so the bound is exact), and the DOP assembly is the same kernel cross-checked against gnss_lib_py in tests/dop_reference.rs. WHY THIS KIND EXISTS: the module behind it has been in the engine and checked against an independent DOP path since L08/L09, but it was not reachable from a run — no kind, no dispatch arm, no bundled file. The README advertised the capability and the verification matrix carried NO row for it at all, so it was simultaneously claimed in prose and unclaimed in the ledger, while being unreachable in the engine. The defaults are the geometry that already carries a committed golden (a user at -80 deg with a 2 m antenna, three beacons at -80/0, -79/+60 and -79/-60 at 2 km, a six-satellite illustrative LCNS snapshot at t=0, a 5 deg mask), so a bare run reproduces a table an oracle already covers rather than inventing fresh numbers. MODELLED: the constellation design, the beacon placement and every error-budget magnitude are illustrative inputs, not a fielded survey or a measured link; only the DOP arithmetic, the horizon closed form and the sigma = DOP x sigma_URE relation are externally anchored. Not a service-performance commitment.
scenarios.toml:
# Surface-beacon augmentation of a lunar orbital navigation service.
#
# A south-polar lunar user sees a sparse orbital constellation inside a narrow, slowly
# moving patch of sky. Every line of sight points into roughly the same direction, so the
# ranging design matrix is ill-conditioned and the dilution of precision is large — the
# geometry problem, not a signal-power problem. A handful of SURVEYED SURFACE BEACONS fix
# it cheaply: a beacon near the local horizon contributes the low-elevation, wide-azimuth
# line-of-sight rows an all-overhead orbital set structurally cannot supply, and the
# horizontal DOP collapses.
#
# This run reports three configurations at one epoch, so the two routes to usable geometry
# can be compared directly:
#
#   * the satellites alone,
#   * the satellites plus whichever beacons clear the horizon, and
#   * a larger constellation instead — the expensive alternative to the same end.
#
# Each row carries its visible-source counts, its full DOP, and the realised 1-sigma
# accuracy in METRES. That last step is the point: a bare "PDOP 1.6" is dimensionless and
# easy to over-read, so the report multiplies it through a per-beacon user-equivalent
# ranging error (the root-sum-square of the clock-synchronisation, multipath and survey
# terms below) and states the answer as a distance.
#
# WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
# The module behind this kind has been in the engine since L08/L09 and is checked against
# an independent DOP path in tests/validate_p2_beacon_before_after_independent_dop.rs. But
# it was not reachable from a run — no scenario kind, no dispatch arm, no bundled example.
# The README advertised the capability; the verification matrix carried NO row for it at all.
# So it was claimed in prose, unclaimed in the ledger, and unreachable in the engine at the
# same time. A capability the engine cannot be ASKED to perform is not a capability of the
# engine, and one the ledger does not list is not accounted for either.
#
# DEFAULTS ARE THE GOLDEN GEOMETRY
# Every value below is the configuration that already carries a committed golden
# (tests/validate_p2_beacon_before_after_table.rs against
# tests/fixtures/lunar_service/beacon_before_after_golden.csv). Running this file therefore
# reproduces a table an oracle already covers, instead of inventing a fresh configuration
# whose numbers nothing checks. Change them freely — they are inputs, not constants.
#
# WHAT IS ANCHORED AND WHAT IS NOT
# Anchored: the DOP assembly is the kernel cross-checked against gnss_lib_py in
# tests/dop_reference.rs; beacon visibility is the airless-Moon two-height geometric horizon
# closed form (no atmosphere, so there is no refractive extension and the bound is exact);
# and sigma = DOP x sigma_URE is the standard relation (Kaplan & Hegarty, Understanding
# GPS/GNSS, section 7).
# NOT anchored — MODELLED inputs, every one: the constellation design, the beacon
# placement, the antenna heights, and all three error-budget magnitudes. They are
# representative choices, not a fielded survey or a measured link. Nothing here is a
# service-performance commitment, a TRL claim, or affiliated with any agency's programme.

kind = "lunar-beacon"

# EVERY SCALAR KEY MUST STAY ABOVE THE [[beacons]] ARRAY BELOW.
# In TOML, a bare key after an array-of-tables header belongs to that TABLE, not to the
# document root. These keys were originally written underneath [[beacons]] and were
# therefore parsed as fields of the LAST beacon, where serde silently dropped them: the
# scenario ran entirely on its defaults, and because the defaults matched what was written
# here, every printed number looked correct. `deny_unknown_fields` on BeaconSite now makes
# that mistake an error instead of silence, and
# tests/lunar_beacon_scenario_reference.rs asserts the parsed scenario really carries
# these values.

# A sparse six-satellite service, and a 24-satellite service as the contrast.
n_satellites = 6
comparison_n_satellites = 24
epoch_s = 0.0
elevation_mask_deg = 5.0

# Per-beacon ranging error budget, in metres of range. Root-sum-squared into sigma_URE.
clock_sync_m = 1.0
multipath_m = 0.5
survey_m = 0.3

# The user: a south-polar site with a 2 m antenna.
[user]
lat_deg = -80.0
lon_deg = 0.0
alt_m = 2.0

# Three surveyed beacons on 2 km relief, spread in azimuth about the user. The two flanking
# sites at +/-60 deg longitude are what supply the wide-azimuth rows.
[[beacons]]
lat_deg = -80.0
lon_deg = 0.0
alt_m = 2000.0

[[beacons]]
lat_deg = -79.0
lon_deg = 60.0
alt_m = 2000.0

[[beacons]]
lat_deg = -79.0
lon_deg = -60.0
alt_m = 2000.0

scenarios.desc: Lunar DIFFERENTIAL PNT — a lunar DGNSS / SBAS analogue.
scenarios.kindDesc: Modelled lunar DIFFERENTIAL PNT (a lunar DGNSS/SBAS analogue): a NovaMoon-class reference station at a KNOWN selenographic location computes per-satellite differential corrections from an ILLUSTRATIVE, public-source Moonlight/LCNS-class constellation (NovaMoon referenced only as a system CLASS, not affiliated with ESA), and a user offset by baseline_km applies them so the COMMON-MODE orbit + clock errors cancel. The clock term cancels EXACTLY (an algebraic identity); the orbit term leaves only the line-of-sight-difference projection, which → 0 as baseline → 0 (the spatial-decorrelation floor) and grows ≈ linearly with baseline. Reports the user 3-D position error WITH vs WITHOUT corrections, the reduction factor, the error-vs-baseline curve, and a user protection level that REUSES the DO-229E SBAS machinery (crate::sbas) with the differential residual σ. MODELLED — exact cancellation identity + first-order decorrelation model; not real-data validated; no TRL/heritage/agency endorsement. Deterministic if seeded.
scenarios.toml:
# Lunar DIFFERENTIAL PNT — a lunar DGNSS / SBAS analogue.
#
# A NovaMoon-class reference station at a KNOWN selenographic location computes
# per-satellite differential corrections from an ILLUSTRATIVE Moonlight / LCNS-class
# constellation; a roving user offset from it by baseline_km applies those corrections so
# the COMMON-MODE broadcast-ephemeris errors (orbit + clock) cancel.
#
# THE IDENTITY (what src/lunar_dpnt.rs implements):
#   ref_error_i      = -e_i . u_ref_i  + c_i           (the correction the station broadcasts)
#   user_raw_i       = -e_i . u_user_i + c_i
#   corrected_user_i = user_raw_i - correction_i = -e_i . (u_user_i - u_ref_i)
# The clock term c_i CANCELS EXACTLY (it is identical in both observations); the orbit
# term collapses to the projection onto the DIFFERENCE of the two line-of-sight unit
# vectors, which -> 0 as the baseline -> 0 (the spatial-decorrelation floor) and grows
# ~linearly with baseline. Mapping the corrected per-satellite range errors through the
# user geometry (a weighted-least-squares snapshot solve) gives the user POSITION error.
#
# NovaMoon is referenced only as a system CLASS (a public description of a lunar reference
# station); the constellation reuses the illustrative public-source LCNS-class set. These
# are illustrative parameters for exercising the differential method, NOT a real ephemeris,
# and imply NO affiliation, endorsement, heritage, certification or TRL.
#
# HONESTY: MODELLED. The common-mode cancellation is an EXACT algebraic identity; the
# spatial-decorrelation residual is a FIRST-ORDER geometric model (the LOS-difference
# projection of an injected orbit error), not a fitted decorrelation model from real lunar
# tracking. The user protection level REUSES the DO-229E SBAS protection-level machinery
# (crate::sbas) with the differential residual sigma as the per-satellite error budget.
# Deterministic given the seed. No real-data validation; no TRL/heritage/agency endorsement.
kind = "lunar-differential-pnt"

# Illustrative LCNS-class constellation (public-source approximation; not affiliated).
n_sats = 8
sma_km = 9737.4        # ~8000 km perilune altitude above the mean lunar radius
eccentricity = 0.6
inc_deg = 57.7
argp_deg = 90.0        # apolune over the southern hemisphere (south-pole favouring)

# NovaMoon-class reference station at a known south-polar selenographic location.
ref_lat_deg = -89.0
ref_lon_deg = 0.0

# User offset from the reference station along the surface (the baseline).
baseline_km = 50.0

# Injected COMMON-MODE per-satellite broadcast errors (the errors the correction removes).
orbit_err_m = 100.0    # orbit-error vector magnitude (random direction per satellite)
clock_err_m = 30.0     # clock error in range units (random sign per satellite)
noise_m = 0.0          # per-receiver measurement noise (0 => exact cancellation at 0 baseline)

seed = 42
t_s = 0.0              # epoch (seconds past the MCI/MCMF-aligned epoch)

# Differential residual sigma fed to the SBAS DO-229E protection-level reuse.
residual_sigma_m = 5.0
p_hmi = 1e-4           # integrity-risk budget (interface parity; DO-229E K-factors fixed)

# ── THE CORRECTION LINK ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The identity above assumes a PERFECT correction: computed by a station that knows
# exactly where it stands, delivered instantly, at infinite resolution. None of the three
# holds, and the three inputs below model what each costs. They feed the `correction_link`
# block of the result document ONLY -- with all three at the values written here, every
# number this scenario emitted before they existed is bit-for-bit unchanged.
#
# 1. SURVEY ERROR. The station forms its correction against the coordinate it BELIEVES.
#    An error there rides on every correction it broadcasts and reaches the user as
#    -delta . u_ref -- which contains no user geometry at all, so unlike the orbit term it
#    neither vanishes at zero baseline nor grows with baseline, and it transfers about
#    one-for-one into the user's position. Default 0.30 m is the crate's own lunar
#    reference-frame position-realisation allocation (lunar_time_budget frame_pos_error_m),
#    itself MODELLED: no lunar surface station has a published surveyed accuracy.
survey_sigma_m = 0.30      # reference-station 3-D coordinate 1-sigma (m), isotropic

# 2. CORRECTION AGEING. A correction computed at t and applied at t+tau is stale two ways.
#    Orbit: the satellite has MOVED, so the frozen orbit-error vector now projects onto a
#    rotated line of sight; the rotation comes from this crate's own propagator, so no
#    orbit-error rate is assumed anywhere. Clock: the satellite clock has drifted by
#    c*sigma_y(tau)*tau for the full-RAFS power law in crate::clock_specs, calibrated there
#    to a published one-day spec row. ILLUSTRATIVE default -- no lunar correction link has
#    a published latency -- which is why the report also emits a 0-300 s latency curve.
latency_s = 10.0           # age of the correction when the user applies it (s)

# 3. QUANTIZATION. The correction crosses a finite-rate link. The quantizer range is NOT a
#    free parameter: it is +/-(orbit_err_m + clock_err_m), an exact bound on the correction
#    magnitude for the injected error model, so the step is 2*(100+30)/2^bits = 1.0156 m at
#    8 bits and the residual variance is the uniform quantizer's step^2/12. The bit count
#    itself is an ILLUSTRATIVE input; 0 disables the term.
quantization_bits = 8      # bits per transmitted correction

scenarios.desc: Seven-parameter Helmert lunar frame datum driven by a SIMULATED OBSERVING CAMPAIGN (G9).
scenarios.kindDesc: Seven-parameter Helmert (similarity) frame datum driven by a SIMULATED OBSERVING CAMPAIGN rather than by an injected transform. A network of Earth stations observes a catalogue of lunar-surface beacons over an explicit schedule; the lunar-VLBI delay partials are accumulated over that schedule into a beacon-coordinate Fisher information matrix exactly as lunar-vlbi-fim does; and that information is propagated through the Helmert design A = [I3 | [p]_x | p] at the catalogue points into the datum covariance H = A^T M_b A, diagnosed by crate::fim::crlb. NO transform is injected and nothing is recovered from a planted answer, so the reported datum accuracy derives from the observing programme: halving the delay sigma halves it exactly, and lengthening the arc improves it because the libration the report MEASURES (sub_earth_direction_sweep_deg) is what separates the line-of-sight beacon coordinate from the plane-of-sky ones. Rank, datum defect, condition number, the full spectrum, the unobservable directions IN THE SEVEN-PARAMETER BASIS, the weakest direction even at full rank and each parameter's share of it are emitted on every run; a parameter the campaign does not constrain is published as NULL with a status, never read out of a near-singular inverse. Beacon-error correlation is measured, not assumed: with the stations held fixed no observation touches two beacons so the information matrix is exactly block-diagonal (offblock_fraction 0), and with the stations estimated the Schur-marginalised block is coupled, with the induced correlation printed and the whole propagation re-run with it discarded so the price of an independence assumption is a number. The same propagation under an isotropic per-coordinate sigma, and the recovery error the lunar-frame-realisation scenario reports, are both run here and printed beside the campaign value with their ratios. MODELLED: the beacon catalogue is sourced but the CAMPAIGN is simulated — the station network and the delay sigma are illustrative inputs, individual delay observations are treated as independent, and the Moon-centre ephemeris, station clocks, troposphere and Earth-orientation parameters are held FIXED, so the datum covariance is a Cramer-Rao bound for a reduced parameter set. Not a geodetic product.
scenarios.toml:
# Seven-parameter Helmert lunar frame datum driven by a SIMULATED OBSERVING CAMPAIGN (G9).
#
# The lunar-frame-realisation scenario injects a known similarity transform and recovers
# it — a solver unit test wearing the clothes of a result. This kind removes the planted
# answer: a network of Earth stations observes a catalogue of lunar-surface beacons over an
# explicit schedule, the lunar-VLBI delay partials are accumulated over that schedule into
# a beacon-coordinate Fisher information matrix exactly as lunar-vlbi-fim does, and that
# information is propagated through the Helmert design A = [I3 | [p]_x | p] at the
# catalogue points into the datum covariance H = A^T M_b A.
#
# Nothing is recovered from a planted transform, so the reported datum accuracy derives
# from the observing programme: halving the delay sigma halves it exactly, and lengthening
# the arc improves it because the libration the report MEASURES
# (sub_earth_direction_sweep_deg) is what separates the line-of-sight beacon coordinate
# from the plane-of-sky ones.
#
# Beacon-error correlation is MEASURED, not assumed. With the stations held fixed no
# observation touches two beacons, so the information matrix is exactly block-diagonal
# (offblock_fraction 0); with the stations estimated the Schur-marginalised block is
# coupled, the induced correlation is printed, and the whole propagation is re-run with it
# discarded so the price of an independence assumption is a number rather than a claim.
#
# The same propagation under an isotropic per-coordinate sigma, and the recovery error the
# lunar-frame-realisation scenario reports, are both run here and printed beside the
# campaign value with their ratios.
#
# MODELLED: the beacon catalogue is sourced but the CAMPAIGN is simulated — the station
# network and the delay sigma are illustrative inputs, individual delay observations are
# treated as independent, and the Moon-centre ephemeris, station clocks, troposphere and
# Earth-orientation parameters are held FIXED. Not a geodetic product.

kind = "lunar-frame-campaign"

scenarios.desc: Lunar reference-frame realisation — a 7-parameter Helmert (similarity) datum fit.
scenarios.kindDesc: Modelled lunar reference-frame realisation: a 7-parameter Helmert (similarity) datum fit — 3 translation, 3 small-angle rotation, 1 scale — tying an estimated set of selenographic-derived MCMF point coordinates to a datum by weighted least squares (crate::batch_ls::gauss_newton), plus a simple orientation tie expressing the realised small rotation about the ICRF axes relative to the IAU 2015 WGCCRE body orientation. The scenario injects a known small transform (translation ~tens of m, rotation ~µrad, scale ~1e-7) into a well-spread synthetic point network, adds seeded Gaussian noise, recovers the datum, and reports the recovered transform, the per-parameter recovery error vs the injected truth, and the post-fit RMS residual. MODELLED self-consistency — recovers an injected similarity transform (noiseless to ~machine precision), NOT a realisation against real tracking/VLBI data; deterministic (seeded); no TRL/heritage/agency endorsement.
scenarios.toml:
# Lunar reference-frame realisation — a 7-parameter Helmert (similarity) datum fit.
#
# Where src/lunar_frame.rs APPLIES the IAU 2015 WGCCRE lunar body orientation (a forward model),
# src/lunar_frame_realise.rs ESTIMATES (realises) a lunar reference frame from a network of point
# coordinates tied to a datum. The estimation core is a classic 7-parameter similarity transform
# mapping points p_i (estimated frame) to q_i (datum frame):
#
#     q_i = t + (1 + s) * R(theta) * p_i
#
# with translation t (m), scale s (dimensionless, ~1e-6 level) and the small rotation
# R(theta) = rz(theta_z) * ry(theta_y) * rx(theta_x). The seven parameters
# [tx, ty, tz, theta_x, theta_y, theta_z, s] are estimated from >= 3 non-collinear point pairs by
# weighted least squares via crate::batch_ls::gauss_newton (forward model flattens every q_i over
# all three components; weights = 1/sigma^2; x0 = zeros). A small orientation tie expresses the
# realised small rotation about the ICRF axes (relative to the IAU body orientation).
#
# THIS SCENARIO injects a KNOWN small Helmert transform (translation ~tens of m, rotation ~uradian,
# scale ~1e-7) into a well-spread synthetic point network (varied selenographic lat/lon mapped to
# MCMF, some points at altitude), adds seeded Gaussian noise, recovers the datum with helmert_fit,
# and reports the recovered transform, the per-parameter recovery error vs the injected truth, and
# the post-fit RMS residual.
#
# Honesty: MODELLED self-consistency. The oracle is the recovery of an injected 7-parameter
# similarity transform (noiseless to ~machine precision) plus the algebraic round-trip identity of
# apply_helmert. This is NOT a realisation of the lunar reference frame against real tracking / VLBI
# data and claims no absolute frame accuracy. Deterministic (seeded). No TRL, flight heritage or
# agency endorsement is claimed.
kind = "lunar-frame-realisation"

# Number of well-spread selenographic network points (>= 3).
n_points = 8

# Injected (truth) translation (m).
tx_m = 25.0
ty_m = -40.0
tz_m = 15.0

# Injected (truth) small rotation (micro-radians).
rot_x_urad = 3.0
rot_y_urad = -2.0
rot_z_urad = 5.0

# Injected (truth) scale (parts-per-billion; 100 ppb = 1e-7).
scale_ppb = 100.0

# Per-coordinate measurement noise standard deviation (m); weights = 1/sigma^2.
noise_sigma_m = 1.0

# Deterministic seed (measurement noise).
seed = 42

# Epoch (UTC) for the ICRF orientation tie.
epoch_year = 2024
epoch_month = 1
epoch_day = 1

REUSES the crate's CCSDS OEM 2.0 emitter+parser (crate::oem) re-tagged for the lunar context — the OEM REF_FRAME carries the IAU 2015 WGCCRE lunar body frame (MOON_ME / MOON_PA), TIME_SYSTEM the lunar time scale (LTC / TCL / UTC), CENTER_NAME = MOON — over a sample illustrative LCNS-class ephemeris (positions from crate::lunar_service, velocity by finite difference). scenarios.toml:
# Lunar interoperability export — LunaNet / IOAG-aligned, CCSDS-based interchange.
#
# Exports the lunar reference frame, the lunar time scale and a lunar ephemeris in
# CCSDS-based interchange forms, with round-trip / field conformance as the oracle.
#
# WHAT src/lunar_interop.rs does:
#   * export_lunar_oem  — REUSES the crate's CCSDS OEM 2.0 emitter (crate::oem),
#     re-tagged for the lunar context: REF_FRAME = the IAU 2015 WGCCRE lunar body
#     frame (MOON_ME / MOON_PA), TIME_SYSTEM = the lunar time scale (LTC / TCL / UTC),
#     CENTER_NAME = MOON, over a sample ILLUSTRATIVE LCNS-class ephemeris (positions
#     from crate::lunar_service, velocity by central finite difference).
#   * export_lunar_time_metadata — a LunaNet/IOAG-aligned lunar-time descriptor (scale
#     id, secular rate µs/day from crate::lunar_time, the published 56-59 µs/day band,
#     reference surface) that round-trips via serde_json.
#   * export_kif_lunar — wraps the OEM + time descriptor + frame label in the existing
#     KIF envelope (crate::interchange) with the MODELLED honesty label.
#   * oem_conformance — checks the required CCSDS/LunaNet header fields are present, the
#     REF_FRAME/TIME_SYSTEM carry the expected lunar tokens, the META_START..META_STOP
#     framing and the position+velocity data lines are well-formed.
#
# HONESTY: MODELLED. The field NAMES and units are aligned with PUBLIC standards
# (CCSDS 502.0-B OEM, IAU WGCCRE 2015 lunar frames, LunaNet Interoperability
# Specification / IOAG lunar architecture). The deterministic round-trip and the
# field-name conformance are the oracle. This is NOT a certified interoperability
# conformance test. The ephemeris is illustrative, public-source, NOT affiliated with
# ESA, and implies no TRL / heritage / agency endorsement.
kind = "lunar-interop-export"

# Lunar body frame: MOON_ME (mean-Earth / polar-axis) or MOON_PA (principal-axis).

# Lunar time scale tag: LTC (Lunar Coordinate Time), TCL or UTC (the Earth tie).

# Sample ephemeris grid.
n_states = 9
step_min = 30.0

# Informational epoch label (the OEM grid hangs off a fixed deterministic epoch).

# Object name written to the OEM OBJECT_NAME / OBJECT_ID.
